Constraint Handling Rules is a constraint logic programming language that enables the definition of complex conditional constraints with built-in procedures. The language's head constraints are grounded in multi-way relations over atoms within a domain, allowing for the definition of complex constraints with built-in procedures that can significantly amplify the expressive power of CHR. The number of atoms in the head of a rule plays a significant role in determining the level of expressive power achieved; as such, we introduce a new CHR variant that allows for heads consisting of a single atom, thereby simplifying the head constraint structure and making it more accessible to researchers and practitioners. The enhanced version facilitates the implementation of complex constraints that can be defined in terms of a single predicate. As a result, we provide a more efficient means of modeling complex problems and demonstrate its applicability to a real-world problem, the train arbitration problem, that can now be modeled using finite state automata.

We investigated how the orientation of the galaxy spin direction dipole changes with redshift and mass, and how it aligns with the direction of light from these galaxies. We analyzed data from the 2MASS (all infrared galaxies), WISE (infrared galaxies), and SDSS (optical galaxies) surveys to compare our findings with those from the KiDS weak lensing study, and our results show a strong consistency in the orientation of the spin direction dipoles across the four surveys, with discrepancies less than 10 degrees. We also found that the direction of the spin direction dipoles remains relatively consistent up to a redshift of around 0.4, and that more massive galaxies generally show a stronger dipoles orientation. Furthermore, we estimated the mass of the underlying matter using our dipole orientation measurements, and our results suggest that more massive galaxies generally reside in darker matter halos.

We introduce a new method, Eigen-Reptile, that efficiently finds the optimal solution in the space of low-dimensional product forms for multi-linear problems. This approach is particularly well-suited for solving problems that can be represented in product form, such as those resulting from few-shot learning. By utilizing the Reptile method, which updates the base of a matrix to optimize the solution, Eigen-Reptile tackles two significant challenges of few-shot learning: insufficient data sampling and label noise. Unlike traditional Reptile, which relies on second-order approximations of the loss function, Eigen-Reptile leverages the top-$t$ eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of the model's outputs to find a more accurate and stable solution. As a result, Eigen-Reptile requires only a fraction of the gradient computations of traditional methods, achieving this while matching or even surpassing their performance on various problems.

To identify novel biomarkers associated with Alzheimer's disease using
Mortality data, we designed a two-part study framework. First, we developed
a machine learning algorithm to forecast the onset of cognitive decline from
individual patient data, even if a diagnosis hasn't been made yet. This model
was then integrated into the main study, where we collected and analyzed the
results for 136 AD patients and 248 non-AD patients. Our study found that the
average age at the time of the Mini-Mental State Examination was a reliable
indicator of cognitive decline from Alzheimer's disease with 83% accuracy. 
Notably, individuals with Alzheimer's disease who had a Mini-Mental State
Examination score below 24 were 6.7 times more likely to experience cognitive
decline than those who didn't have the condition. Meanwhile, non-Alzheimer's
patients with extremely low Mini-Mental State Examination scores were 2.9
times more likely to experience cognitive decline than their healthy counterparts.

This paper assesses the current understanding in AI Ethics research, focusing on analyses of fairness, accountability, and transparency in AI systems. A comprehensive examination of 714 publications revealed that AI Ethics research has matured, utilizing established frameworks and methodologies to evaluate AI systematically. However, these findings also highlight areas requiring improvement, such as the lack of empirical analysis and standardized evaluation methods across the field. To foster growth, we propose a new model that differentiates various levels of ethical AI analysis and emphasizes the need for nuanced case studies. Ultimately, our ethical analysis framework aims to support researchers in developing tailored ethics assessments across diverse AI systems.

The study of language families, which are subsets of the infinite words over ω, is an area of interest. In this context, researchers have been exploring the possibility of identifying a unique and essential member in each nonempty set of language families, which are closed under certain operations. A family of languages is considered essential if its essential member is an element of every such family. A recent paper by Colcombet, Genest, Pirutka, and Pirutka found a significant application in the study of languages. According to the findings, the essential member in the family of Boolean-closed full trios is the family of B\'{e}zout languages, which is also true for other counting-based operations. This study has been extended to cover the infinite words over two non-negative integers. It was shown that the essential member in the family of Boolean-closed full trios is the family of B\'{e}zout two-counting languages, which is also true for any given integer. This result has also been proven to hold for any higher number of counts. This achievement has also led to a new discovery of the essential member in the family of Boolean-closed full syzygies, which is also related to counting-based operations. A low-complexity approach to estimating hybrid beam-based channels involves using a two-stage estimation method that combines a low-complexity beam prediction technique, which is an improvement over a previously reported estimation method, and a deep neural network that refines channel estimates by accounting for beam correlations. The improved beam prediction technique, which is an enhancement over a previous approach, utilizes a greedy algorithm that is trained using simulated channel data. The proposed deep neural network architecture incorporates both convolutional and fully connected layers to learn channel statistics in both time and spatial domains. It is trained using real channel data. Simulation results reveal that the proposed estimation method achieves a lower root mean square error in channel estimation than the conventional single stage estimation method. Consequently, this yields a substantial improvement in downlink rate.

Recent discrepancies in V_{ud} and V_{us} measurements pose significant challenges to the Standard Model of physics. The anomalies of V_{ud} and V_{us} individually have limited potential to test new physics since they can often be explained by a single model. In contrast, together they offer a more comprehensive understanding. We investigate the potential of future measurements to thoroughly understand the sources of these anomalies. Theoretical predictions for short-distance functions in the neutrino sector are crucial in resolving the V_{ud} and V_{ud} anomalies. Theoretical input is necessary to interpret future measurements of neutrino decay and charged-current neutrino scattering. We present an enhanced version of the U-Net [1] architecture, specifically designed for semantic segmentation of MRI data acquired through 3D volumes. The proposed network incorporates 3D operations from the beginning, unlike the initial U-Net which employed 2D operations. Furthermore, our 3D U-Net architecture incorporates dilated or atypical kernels in convolution layers to maximize available receptive fields and mitigate the risk of overfitting with fewer parameters. The 3D U-Net architecture is implemented on the BRAIN-DR dataset [2], which contains 3D MRI data for individuals with Diabetes and diverse anatomies. The results show that our 3D U-Net significantly outperforms the 2D U-Net with an improvement of 26% in terms of Dice coefficient and a reduction of 17% in cross-entropy loss.

We have developed an innovative method for achieving formal data privacy without relying on sensitive data categorization. Instead, we utilize a combination of utility data views, private views, and a learning algorithm that can be applied to both utility and private views. The private views are generated based on a set of rules that eliminate data attributes that might indirectly reveal sensitive information, effectively separating private and shared information through transformation. The challenges associated with traditional learning algorithms are addressed by employing a combination of loss regularization and distribution distillation to train two separate neural networks, one for each view, using a tailored learning rate schedule. The private view is trained using a combination of distillation and a loss term that prevents attribute leakage, while the private and utility view distributions are compared to ensure distribution equivalence and a maintained level of utility. The results from extensive experiments on real and synthetic data demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in achieving both theoretical and practical data privacy without requiring knowledge of sensitive attributes, offering a novel application scenario.

We have developed a novel method for determining the contribution of dust heating from active galactic nuclei (AGN) in nearby galaxies through a comparison of infrared and radio emissions. By applying this approach to 21 nearby galaxies with high-infrared-brightness AGN using data from the Spitzer Space Telescope images, we observed a notable pattern of excess dust heating in galaxies with intense radio activity and certain morphological characteristics. The findings suggest that the primary source of hot dust emission is likely AGN activity rather than non-thermal processes, and we identify the underlying causes of the observed hot dust anomaly. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our results for the understanding of dust heating in nearby galaxies with low levels of infrared emission.

Recent advancements in large language models have enabled them to process complex natural language inputs and produce human-like responses through tailored prompts. Nevertheless, the current methods for crafting prompts are largely based on intuition rather than a deep understanding of the task at hand. This paper proposes MORALCOT, a prompt generation framework that utilizes causal graph theory and moral reasoning to create more effective prompts in a dialogue setting. We demonstrate that MORALCOT outperforms existing approaches in moral reasoning by incorporating key aspects of human moral argumentation, such as the consideration of consequences and the application of principles.

We show that a valuation ring $R$ with a residue field of characteristic $p$ can be represented as the inductive limit of a system of $p$-homogeneous Lie algebras through a process that preserves their Poisson-Lie structure. This method is demonstrated using the Hodge algebra associated to a quiver $Q$.

The two-dimensional Dirac equation has significant importance across various domains of physics including high-energy, condensed matter, and materials science. We derive a comprehensive solution set for the free and mass-corrected 2D Dirac equation in scalar-symmetric electrodynamics, displaying the general expression's capability to encompass Dirac equations encompassing numerous spin-orbit interactions and external potentials. We then proceed to explore particular instances of this solution, encompassing an in-depth discussion of the spinless cases, the Dirac equation in a magnetic field, and other related scenarios.

In cooperative driving settings, individual vehicles can benefit from the actions of their companions, leading to enhanced performance using techniques like Model Predictive Control (MPC). However, these control methods rely on perfect model knowledge, which is not always the case in real-world driving. This paper investigates the use of multi-agent MPC for cooperative tasks, focusing on scenario where a lead vehicle aids a follower vehicle. It examines how model inaccuracies propagate through the predictive horizon and presents an adaptive approach to mitigate this issue. Evaluations using a simplified automotive test case demonstrate the effects of model inaccuracies on predictive horizons and the efficacy of the proposed method.

The widespread dissemination of information on the internet has created challenges in identifying and differentiating authentic from fake content. This study combines machine learning and natural language processing techniques to analyze online news articles and their source credibility based on social media platform opinions. By examining the interplay between sources of information and their corresponding social media mentions, we aim to develop an effective approach to evaluate information credibility. Given that social media can help gauge public opinion on the credibility of information shared online, we explored three aspects - amount, interaction, and mention time - to characterize social media mentions as features for classification. Our approach was applied to a dataset of news articles and their corresponding social media interactions on Twitter, which was used to train a classifier to assess information credibility. Our results demonstrate that incorporating social media mention features significantly enhances the accuracy of the classification model, with the best results achieved when combining the three aspects together.

Ensuring the safety of road users in emergency situations such as crashes or road hazards on networks is a critical aspect for operators of telecommunications systems. To address this, we present a novel framework called $\pi$-ROAD that enables real-time monitoring, detection, and proactive resolution of such incidents by formulating them as a specialized optimization problem. $\pi$-ROAD is designed to handle the dynamic nature of network environments while minimizing the impact of additional resources on network performance. Through mathematical modeling and simulation, we evaluate the effectiveness of $\pi$-ROAD and demonstrate its ability to effectively contain incidents by allocating minimal resources, such as 0.5% of total edge resources, without compromising the overall performance of the network.

This study presents a user-centric approach to creating a versatile platform that seamlessly integrates a human-machine interface with a decision-making system for a multi-robot environment. A human operator's tasks are divided into two segments: (1) setting a trajectory for the robots and (2) establishing safety zones for their collaborative work. A sophisticated control system receives these inputs and ensures the robots navigate through their assigned paths while maintaining a safe distance according to the specified safety zones. Our research is grounded in the development of a multi-robot system utilizing a collision avoidance algorithm, which enables the robots to adjust their speeds to circumvent potential obstacles. However, this approach may lead to robots deviating from their original paths; therefore, we have designed a control system that combines the decision-making and path-planning functions to maintain the original trajectory. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we have implemented it on a Baxter robot in a complex environment. A video of the experiment can be found on YouTube at https://youtu.be/3mYgKZKQr8k.

The ongoing technological revolution is profoundly shaping our urban environments.
Advancements in autonomous vehicles and AI are transforming city layouts, with
self-driving vehicles being a key factor in traffic management, infrastructure,
transportation systems, and overall city design. This study aims to develop a
modular model for the multi-layered traffic ecosystem, integrating various levels
of autonomy through dynamic interaction mechanisms. Our approach is centered around
the development of an information sharing and coordination system, enabling the
integration of autonomous vehicles into interconnected traffic networks. By focusing
on this core aspect, we can create a flexible model for different urban settings,
enabling the implementation of autonomous vehicles in various applications and
solutions within the multi-agent traffic ecosystem.

In this context, we explore two types of online caching problems: the $k$-server problem and the graph bipartite matching problem. For the $k$-server problem, we investigate a new online algorithm that ensures a subpolynomial competitive ratio when the adversary's prediction of demand with an error rate of $\varepsilon$ is feasible. This algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of $O(k\cdot\ell_{\infty}\cdot\ell_{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}})$ where $n$ is the number of servers and $\ell_{\alpha}$ is the $(\alpha)$-average case in a unit disk graph. This result improves upon the existing competitive ratio of $O(k\cdot\ell_{\infty}\cdot\ell_{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon})$. Furthermore, we also show that the existing algorithm has a subpolynomial competitive ratio when the number of servers is constant. For the graph bipartite matching problem, we introduce a new online algorithm that ensures a subpolynomial competitive ratio when the number of servers is constant and the prediction error is bounded by $\varepsilon$. Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in image segmentation tasks, particularly when accompanied by innovative techniques to resolve existing challenges. This paper introduces a novel Trilateral Attention Network that enhances convolutional neural networks by integrating three types of attention, namely spatial, channel, and temporal, through a novel tri-lateral pathway architecture. The proposed Trilateral Attention Network is an end-to-end trainable module that can be seamlessly incorporated into any CNN architecture, offering superior performance in image segmentation tasks. Thorough experiments have been conducted to validate the effectiveness of the Trilateral Attention Network, which outperforms other attention-based methods by leveraging the unique strengths of its three components. Specifically, our analysis reveals that each component contributes to the segmentation performance, with the spatial attention module focusing on spatially localized structures, the channel attention module selecting relevant features, and the temporal attention module aggregating information across time to refine feature extraction.

In superspace with a modified geometry, the torsion constraints are equivalent to the divergence of gauge fields, leading to the existence of locally flat gauge fields throughout the entire space. This implies that locally these fields are described by a single scalar potential, leading to the determination of the properties of the resulting field theories. This includes derivation of the Yang-Mills equations, determination of the current conservation laws, evaluation of the effective action at low energy, derivation of the properties of supermultiplets, and the classification of the fermion fields within these multiplets. This implies that the supergeometry considered has the characteristics of N=1, U(1) supersymmetry.

The quality of training data is a crucial factor for the development of accurate machine learning models. This study introduces an approach that enables the automatic identification and prioritization of unreliable data samples within existing datasets, thereby improving the overall quality of the training data. Our methodology is built upon the principle that the influence of each individual data example on the learning model should be directly related to its contribution to the overall quality of the data. This is achieved by training two separate models: one using the full dataset and the other using a subset of the full dataset known to be reliable. By comparing the performance of these models, we can determine the influence of each data example and thus assess the reliability of the data. Our experimental results, which involved using three datasets from the IMDB website to compare the performance of Support Vector Machines and Neural Networks, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in evaluating data quality.

In a Chern insulator system, we've discovered that quantum pumping of electric charge on the Hall surface can be significantly enhanced when geometric and chiral properties are simultaneously present. A key factor in this increase is the non-abelian matrix Berry phase, which we found to be a key element in this process and not just a pure geometric property as previously thought. To better understand its role, we have modeled the system under both weak and strong magnetic conditions, as well as varying levels of chiral interactions. Furthermore, we have investigated the impact of different coupling strengths on the system's behavior, with a focus on identifying the critical threshold beyond which we observe a rapid change in the pumping phase.

We expand upon the METRO-LM framework by integrating language models with interactive and generative capabilities. By combining scalable attention with sparse attention, we create highly efficient large language models that outperform previous benchmarks in efficiency and accuracy. The METRO-1BTrillion model, specifically a 1.3 trillion parameter model that requires 3x less attention computation than GPT-3, yet has comparable performance to the GPT-3 model. Additionally, our model can be reduced to a minimal version, only 0.5% of its original size, without compromising accuracy in benchmarks such as GLUE, SQuAD, and SNLI. The model's ability to engage in conversation and adapt to unseen examples is also demonstrated, indicating its capability to handle complex tasks beyond its original training data. The source code for our model and tests is available for public access at https://github.com/microsoft/metro.

A quantum network's structure plays a vital role in reliable information transmission. A novel quantum channel coding method, called qubit-vertex coding, enables the distribution of entangled states between two nodes in a fully connected, topologically complex quantum network. This coding method allows users to transmit multiple entangled qubits simultaneously by solely utilizing local measurement tools, thus reducing communication overhead. It offers flexibility in adapting to different network topologies, including random graphs, by achieving a positive scaling relationship in transmitted entangled states' number with respect to the nodes connected to local qubits. This scaling holds even when the connectivity is minimal, providing an alternative method for quantum teleportation.

This paper presents a method for creating knowledge-based explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) tools that can be utilized by individuals with no prior programming knowledge. A novel approach is proposed that combines knowledge graphs to facilitate the understanding of visual encodings, specifically by utilizing a question-answering framework. Our findings indicate that an introductory strategy centered on around top $k$ queries proves to be the most effective in facilitating comprehension. To enhance the usability of our tool, a customized mobile app is developed, and its effectiveness is evaluated through two on-site trials with both technical and non-technical experts, revealing that our method is effective in transferring technical knowledge to non-technical individuals.

We investigate the challenge of controlling quantum systems with optical pulses when they are subject to a periodic heating effect. Due to the complex nature of interacting quantum systems, accurately predicting the outcome of pulse sequences is a difficult task. In contrast, in non-interacting systems, the problem can often be solved analytically. In this work, we demonstrate that the Floquet heating effect can be effectively averaged out by using specific pulse sequences, allowing previously known analytical results to be applied. Furthermore, we show that the optical manipulation of many-body systems is a process that can be effectively controlled using sequences of pulses, and that the desired states can be prepared efficiently.

We investigate the impact of uncertainty in model parameters on the execution of counterfactual plans. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of uncertainty-adjusted counterfactual plans, which take into account model uncertainty to reduce the effects of plan execution risks. To achieve this, we develop an optimization framework incorporating model uncertainty and an approximation technique for scalable deployment. Furthermore, we analyze the computational complexity of our framework and demonstrate its efficacy through real-world experimentation with a robotic manipulation dataset.

This paper introduces a technique that enables the generation of labeled data samples from unlabeled audio recordings and presents their utilization in urban sound classification tasks. The technique works by generating time-frequency representations and assigning labels to each representation based on the surrounding audio context. The resulting labeled data samples are employed to train deep neural networks on data from three datasets, leading to the achievement of superior classification accuracy of 0.39, 0.44, and 0.65 on the ESC-50, US80k, and KFSU datasets respectively, surpassing existing state-of-the-art results on the US80k dataset.

We explore exact $AdS_2 \times S^2$ and $AdS_2 \times H^2$ geometries within the context of $N=4$ gauged supergravity in four dimensions, with a focus on their physical properties. These geometries emerge as a specific limit of $AdS_4$ black holes and serve as a square root of the latter in a particular sense. The holographic boundary conditions for these geometries are examined, and a consistent matching of classical and subleading entropy is achieved by incorporating a horizon into the geometries, thereby extending the boundary entropy calculation.

The Code Analysis Integrated Nexus (Cain) is a new compiler that translates a high-level, block-diagram language into efficient C code. In contrast to other existing compilers, CAIN produces code with significantly less complexity. This is achieved through a novel approach that utilizes a graph optimization algorithm to reduce the size of circuit representations before translating them into C. As a result, CAIN generates code that is substantially shorter than that produced by other compilers, when running on a range of benchmarks from the SCAMP-5 suite.

The Witten effect is expected to be observed in systems where there is a difference in the number of fermions on each side of a partitioning surface in a holographic duality. Current research suggests that this effect has a more intricate relationship with the bulk black hole's properties than initially thought, specifically with regards to its charge. This study examines the impact of a surface separating empty and charged space regions on the black hole's behavior, revealing a more complex interaction than previously understood. By drawing a connection between the Witten effect and the concept of 'backreaction,' it sheds new light on the conventional interpretation of it as a quantum effect. The research also implies that the Witten effect may be more widespread than currently thought, occurring not just in systems with distinct fermion numbers but potentially in all cases involving distinct quantum subregions.

In the realm of online convex optimization over complex spaces, regret minimization is a critical metric. A notable solution, regret pruning, offers a practical and efficient approach for learning Nash equilibria effectively. Two refined versions of this technique have been developed and tested, and results demonstrate that these enhancements outperform the original method.

This paper introduces a novel modal logic with one non-classical model of states and another model of truth to reframe and expand on Aristotle's modal syllogistic from the perspective of possible factual situations. The core aspect of this logic is its ability to define an essential form using only the two basic modal terms "to be" and "not-to be", ultimately leading to a simplified and complete set of rules for syllogisms. The resulting logic enables us to derive all of Aristotle's missing syllogisms, prove all excluded middle and conditional theorems, and establish that the premises in invalid arguments are either always false or always untrue. The resulting formalism reveals the underlying structure of the modal system, allowing for a precise mapping of the modal space and a method to determine the degree of relatedness between two terms.

In quantum mechanics, causal relationships between measurement outcomes can be strongly disallowed, yet achieving this without perfect detection accuracy is only possible in classical systems. A key strategy for testing causal relationships involves using two measurements A and B, followed by a third measurement C that receives information through causality, often requiring the ability to access all data. However, this paper shows that in quantum systems, local causal relationships can be disallowed without limitations on detection accuracy, but still cannot be achieved with finite efficiency. Moreover, if the local measurements A and B experience finite efficiency but the measurement of C does not, then causality becomes possible. A core component of this result is the creation of a set of causal inequalities that can be broken only by quantum systems with finite detection for A and B but infinite detection for C, which is unique to quantum systems and not replicable by classical systems.

This research paper examines how to optimize rate and distortion in video encoding using a dual critic reinforcement learning framework. Currently, state-of-the-art video encoders employ rate-distortion optimization, which balances quality and efficiency but requires extensive training due to numerous parameters. To address this limitation, the authors propose an efficient reinforcement learning framework that treats rate and distortion as separate objectives. They use a dual critic architecture to assess the distance between the encoder's actions between consecutive frames, allowing them to improve constraint satisfaction while maintaining compatibility with existing encoders. This approach enables them to fine-tune pre-trained encoders, yielding performance comparable to models specifically designed for constrained video encoding.

The carbon-rich environment of planetary disks is a key factor in the formation of complex organic molecules. However, the source of the primary light element, carbon, in these disks is unclear. This study investigates the carbon distribution in disks containing carbon-rich grains and gas by accounting for the impact of photo-ablation on grain composition. Through simulations, the study reveals that this process leads to a sustained cycle in which carbon-rich grains lose their surface carbon, which is then released into the gas phase. This equilibrium has a significant effect on the distribution of carbon across the disk, particularly in the outer regions where carbon-rich grains are most abundant. As a result, the distribution of carbon-rich species is significantly altered, with an increase in the carbon abundance relative to hydrogen in the outer disk. This study's findings will be crucial for understanding the carbon distribution in planetary disks and its implications for the formation of complex organic molecules.

In solving mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), selecting a single optimal solution often proves challenging. While modern machine learning methods can improve MILP performance, they typically require substantial time to train and typically only account for a single solution. To address this limitation, we propose NeuralCut, a novel framework that learns to efficiently select multiple high-quality cuts for solving a MILP within a time-bound. We show that NeuralCut can be trained without requiring access to a large collection of MILP solutions. Experimentally, NeuralCut outperforms state-of-the-art methods, requiring significantly less training time while yielding improved solution quality on a range of benchmarks.

The Mo-MoTe$_2$ monolayer in T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_{x}$Te$_{2}$ single crystals serves as a unique platform for exploring exotic quantum phenomena, such as superconductivity and topological properties, despite previous studies indicating that T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_{x}$Te$_{2}$ is a non-superconducting topological insulator for x=0.08. Our research reveals that T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_{x}$Te$_{2}$ becomes a superconductor at a critical x threshold, with a transition temperature increasing with x. This superconducting phase exhibits distinct characteristics, including zero-resistance at low temperatures, a Meissner effect, and a critical field, indicating it is a conventional superconductor. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the superconducting phase in T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_{x}$Te$_{2}$ is driven by a strong electron-phonon coupling. These findings point to a complex phase diagram for T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_{x}$Te$_{2}$, exhibiting a transition from a non-superconducting topological insulator to a conventional BCS superconductor as x increases.

A significant proportion of software issues are repeat occurrences, with research indicating up-to 50% of reports being identical or having a substantial similarity to existing reports. A substantial body of literature has focused on resolving the issue of duplicate report retrieval, although there is a lack of comprehensive studies examining the effectiveness of NLP techniques for duplicate report retrieval across various datasets and feature sets. This study provides an exhaustive evaluation of 15 different NLP-based features, utilizing three datasets, to assess their effectiveness in duplicate report retrieval and compares their performance to that of a baseline method. The study also proposes a novel approach, based on a combination of NLP techniques and information retrieval methods, which outperforms existing models such as Okapi and BERT.

A strongly coupled field theory describing Rarita-Schwinger fields in graphene has been formulated and applied to study phase transitions in this two-dimensional fermi surface, utilizing the functional renormalization group method to calculate the low-energy spectral flow and critical behavior near a quantum critical point. This approach has revealed distinct critical exponents for Rarita-Schwinger critical points, in contrast to the Ginzburg-Landau theory, and has also provided a quantum critical spectrum of dynamical susceptibility, thereby shedding light on the emergence of new excitations at the critical point and their influence on the associated phase transitions.

We propose a self-training teacher-student framework that leverages pseudo labels generated by a teacher model to train a student model. Unlike conventional training methods, our approach is enabled by a novel learning strategy allowing the teacher and student to learn from each other without sharing the same dataset. Furthermore, we introduce a novel class confidences loss that enhances the student's performance by discouraging overconfident predictions. Through our approach, we demonstrate that the student model can achieve results comparable to the teacher model, if not surpass them, by utilizing only 60% of the teacher's dataset. We apply our method to NER models, successfully improving state-of-the-art results on six benchmark datasets.

This paper presents a large dataset of 3,956 US tourism-related queries on Bing, 
gathering data over three years to facilitate in-depth analysis. The research 
is organized into sections, showcasing how various insights derived from this data, 
coupled with advanced analysis and prediction methods, can yield valuable 
knowledge for the travel and hospitality industry, with demonstrated examples 
throughout.

The parameter that governs how effective features of tiny structures impact larger materials is predicted by a machine learning algorithm, using data from thousands of different combinations of tiny structures and their larger counterparts made of the same material. This prediction method is then applied to cases where the size of tiny structures is much smaller or larger than expected.

A recent discovery of a massive Jupiter-like planet known as CI Tau b revealed that it was born outside the star it orbits today, only migrating to its current position. Researchers conducted a thorough analysis of the system using high-resolution imaging techniques, including differential imaging and coronagraphy, to investigate the possibility of the planet's migration. The results showed that the planet's movement cannot be attributed to the star's activity, as existing models would have detected any significant migration signals. Additionally, the team's null detection of CI Tau b at large separations suggests that the planet's migration occurred relatively recently. The team's data also ruled out the possibility of the star having a companion object with a mass of at least 0.5 M, orbiting at a distance of 20 AU. The team's findings provide new insights into the migration timing of CI Tau b, suggesting that the planet migrated within the past 22 million years.
We establish that in a given anisotropic potential, the zero-energy trajectories coincide with the high-energy trajectories of a free motion on a sphere.

In the context of standard variational analysis, we examine a class of elliptic fractional differential equations within bounded domains, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We focus on non-local integro-differential operators that incorporate a non-negative function and a parameter, $p$, greater than zero. Through a comprehensive study, we derive novel existence results for non-trivial solutions, including a proof that a specific class of solutions exhibits an odd symmetry with respect to specific transformations. These findings hold under two distinct conditions on the function $c$: either as a constant, or a function decreasing on the interval (0,1), leading to significant implications for non-standard equations within singular problems.

This study presents a novel approach to estimating trajectories in various environments by combining data from different sensors. We introduce a new generative model that enables the trajectory estimation of multiple objects in scenarios with insufficient or no label data. By leveraging this model, we are able to address and solve the challenging problem of multi-object tracking. We develop a joint model that incorporates the proposed generative model and a new object detection module, allowing for joint inference of object trajectories and classification. We introduce a new sensor-based loss function that improves the performance of the model and achieves state-of-the-art results in trajectory estimation, as well as competitive performance in object detection tasks.

The original stability assessment criterion using angle stability is no longer reliable for modern power systems with high levels of renewable energy integration and power converters, primarily due to inaccuracies in communication with inverter units and limited data exchange among them. A new stability assessment criterion, which relies solely on data from the control systems of power converters, is proposed in this paper. It is assumed that the new criterion can accurately identify stable points, but may misclassify unstable points with a higher probability. To determine this error probability, the paper proposes a method to calculate the communication stability region of a single-coupled dynamical system using the new criterion. Additionally, the paper suggests a more efficient communication protocol that reduces the number of required communication steps, thereby decreasing data exchange among systems. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces communication overhead while providing high accuracy in identifying stable and unstable points.

In recent years, the use of biometric signature verification has gained significant traction, driven by the advancement of digital technology. Signature verification through video-based methods has gained popularity due to their ease of use and adaptability. These methods, which rely on feature extraction from signature templates, are crucial for effective forgery detection, thereby ensuring the robustness of authentication systems. The performance of these signature verification systems hinges on the unique characteristics of the signature templates, which distinguishes them from each other. In this research, we examine the distinctiveness, intricacy, and repeatability of signature templates, and its impact on the efficacy of forgery detection. A novel feature, known as the complexity of signature template, is introduced to measure its intricacy, which is then used to evaluate the distinctiveness of the signature templates. A statistical test is used to measure the repeability of the signature templates, and a visual analysis of the signature templates is employed to evaluate their distinctiveness. The findings of this research demonstrate that the proposed metrics bear a significant positive correlation with the efficacy of forgery detection, thereby highlighting the utility of these measures in evaluating the quality of signature templates.

The standard interpretation of the Hardy sum $H(x,y)$ as a density of plane geodesics is extended to any number of dimensions. In a fixed dimension $n$, geodesics are viewed as infinite sequences of points, and an "oriented" geodesic is considered, where each point is connected by a consistent sign, defined as clockwise in $n$-dimensional space. We calculate the probability that an oriented geodeic never intersect with a randomly selected one moving in a fixed direction, which translates into finding the asymptotic behavior of $H(x,y)$ as $y$ approaches infinity. This research is related to the findings presented in a previous paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06324.

Mobile apps frequently collect context data, such as user location and activity history, through various activities like search queries and movement tracking. This context information can significantly impact mobile application functionality and the overall user experience. Our research focuses on examining the potential of leveraging persistent contextual values to enhance user customization and personalized recommendations. A comprehensive online survey was conducted to investigate the feasibility of this approach, which revealed that: (1) users are willing to share their location and activity history context information, (2) this context can greatly affect app functionality and the user experience, (3) users are open to sharing their context information with other parties when it benefits their personal preferences, (4) users are willing to share their context information with third parties when it benefits their personal preferences, (5) users are willing to share their context information with third parties when it benefits their personal preferences. The survey results will serve as a valuable resource for mobile developers and industry stakeholders to understand how persistent contextual values can be utilized for personalized customization and recommendations.

We present an efficient system for estimating the position, orientation, and scale of 3D objects from 2D images solely using 2D-3D correspondences. The system's core, referred to as Real-Time Object 2D-3D Homography Estimation, achieves real-time performance and accurately maps 2D-3D correspondences to homographies through learning-based pose estimation for objects in various poses. By combining a network that estimates the pose of a primary object with real-time filtering and tracking, our system estimates the position, orientation, and scale of objects in real-time, even in complex scenarios with multiple objects. The system's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/stevepinne/2d-3d-homography.

The Indian multi-wavelength space observatory, AstroSat, has been successfully operational since May 2015. Its three cutting-edge instruments - the LAXPC, SXT, and UVET - provide precise ultraviolet, soft X-ray, and hard X-ray data. A specially designed collimated instrument plays a crucial role in determining the absolute flux of sources observed by AstroSat. It compares data collected from the instrument against simultaneous ground-based measurements to verify its accuracy. So far, the instrument has measured the flux of 19 X-ray sources with a high degree of accuracy, thereby validating its performance. Its robust calibration pipeline and high accuracy make it possible to compare AstroSat data with data collected from other space missions, thereby facilitating the calibration of its energy scale. Its high temporal resolution enables the comparison of AstroSat data with data collected from ground-based instruments, thereby providing an opportunity to study the absolute flux of sources.

This paper presents a comprehensive examination of blockchain technology and its underlying principles. The discussion begins with an overview of notable predecessors and progresses to a detailed analysis of public and private blockchain systems. Several prominent permissioned and permissionless protocols are examined in depth, including Hyperledger Fabric, Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Ethereum Classic. These systems are evaluated in terms of functionality and requirements, with a focus on fabric's modular design and its distinct features. The key characteristics of a blockchain protocol, such as its architecture, consensus mechanisms, and execution environment, are also explored in detail. Furthermore, the discussion delves into the challenges associated with deploying blockchain technology and implementing its integration with existing systems.

A revised version of the spin--mandelstam method has been developed to account for the enhanced chromomagnetic interaction within the framework of the Bethe--Salpeter equation. By incorporating this improvement, the mass spectra of the $X(6900)$, $T_{cc}(3875/3940)$, $Y(4260)$, $Z_c(3900)$, $P_{cs}(4459)$, $P_{cs}(4338)$, $P_{cs}(1630)$, $\eta_1(1855)$, $X(3872)$, and $Y(2260)$ tetraquarks and the $B_c(5620)$ baryon can be successfully calculated, resulting in results that are consistent with existing experimental observations. Moreover, the predicted mass of the $B_c(1)$ baryon will be experimentally confirmed in the near future through the CDF, LHCb, CMS, and/or FCC experiments.

We investigate the theoretical limits of Higgs boson masses within an extension of the Standard Model, specifically the $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_X$ theory. The model incorporates a Higgs triplet and a singlet, along with a dimension-6 operator to address the hierarchy problem. By examining the vacuum expectation value of the triplet, we assess the model's stability, determining that the instability scale's lower bound is significantly increased when the triplet has a non-zero vacuum expectation value. Consequently, this implies that the Higgs boson mass can be increased by up to 4 GeV, thus allowing for compatibility with recent results from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider.

This research delves into the relationships between four distinct equations, namely the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, $p$-Talagrand inequality, $p$-Fermi-Dirac distribution, and a modified $p$-Fermi-Dirac distribution. Specifically, we focus on the general case in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and derive equivalent forms of the four equations, and later we extend this analysis to Carnot groups. Notably, our work expands on existing research in [GGM20] by applying the JKO scheme in metric measure spaces and Carnot groups.

A new estimator, the exponentially weighted divergence estimator, has been developed for a specific statistical function and has been tested within a specific statistical framework. This estimator is a variation of a well-established estimator, derived from a divergence measure known as the exponentially weighted divergence. Our analysis found that this estimator outperforms another existing estimator, both in terms of its convergence characteristics and its sensitivity to data outliers. A comprehensive study was also conducted to evaluate the performance of this new estimator under varying sample sizes, comparison measures, and data dimensions. The results from this study demonstrate the estimator's robustness.

We aim to develop an advanced image compression algorithm that integrates AI 
capabilities to process dynamic image areas. Our method starts by identifying the 
key areas within an image that prioritize motion and distinguishes them from 
stationary elements. By assigning different labels to pixels, we enable a neural 
network to process static and motion-centric elements using customized 
algorithms. Our technique successfully separates static and motion areas even when 
the motion is not currently present, resulting in more precise image decoding. 
Additionally, we propose a novel quantization process that preserves the critical 
spatial details necessary for high-quality image reconstruction. Our method can 
flexibly process various image types, including static and dynamic video as well 
as mixed images that combine static and motion elements. By incorporating a learned 
disentangled representation, we achieve superior compression results on high 
resolution videos compared to other state-of-the-art video compression algorithms.

In our research, we are examining how the dynamics of periodic orbits affect the statistics of eigenvalues in a class of complex systems known as quantum graphs. These graphs are composed of interconnected loops that intersect in a repeating pattern, and we're interested in how the unique geometry of these graphs influences the statistics of eigenvalue coefficients. We've found that for a family of these graphs with varying connection strengths, the coefficients' variance increases as the number of intersecting loops rises, regardless of the system size. This phenomenon stands in contrast to non-intersecting graphs, where we've found that their eigenvalue coefficients' variance is largely unaffected by system size.

The periodic variable stars are categorized into six groups, namely eclipsing binaries, nebular variables, reflection variables, pulsating variables, pulsating giants, and others, based on their light curves. In the classification of periodic variables, eclipsing binaries and nebular variables are distinguished by their maximum amplitudes and periods. Our study focuses on a sample of 150,000 periodic variables from the OGLE-IV survey and employs a multi-step approach to separate eclipsing binaries from other periodic variables using their amplitude and period characteristics. Our methodology leverages the 3D-VOF density distribution to identify the distinct classes of periodic variables and allows for the precise identification of nebular variables. Our findings reveal that approximately 70% of classified variables align with our expectations, while the remaining 30% require further analysis to determine their classification. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of periodic variables and offers insights into their nature and distribution.

This paper proposes a novel method for determining the nearest negative imaginary system from a given time-invariant system. Notably, the proposed approach can be obtained by scaling a non-negative imaginary system using either real-time or complex-time metrics. Additionally, the method encompasses the concepts of negative imaginary and passive systems. These findings are supported by examples, including the Kalmann-Yacoub system.

The primary objective of continual learning is to improve performance on sequential tasks by retaining prior knowledge. However, this goal is challenging due to forgetting previously learned tasks, which hampers performance on previous tasks when exposed to new tasks. This paper investigates how well continual learning methods perform on End-to-End automatic speech recognition (ESR) tasks by comparing the performance of various methods. The comparison includes fine-tuning, Pseudo-Continual Learning, and three additional methods: the Early Fine-tuning method, the Elastic Weight Consolidation method, and the the Synaptic-Interference Continual Learning method. The results show that, although the Continual Learning methods perform relatively well, there is a significant performance gap between the best Continual Learning method and fine-tuning, which achieves up to 5.2% better results on the new task. The absence of baseline methods for pre-training and limited training data availability in ESR tasks may have contributed to this significant performance gap.

Social media data often exhibit code-switching, switching between languages like English and Spanish in tweets, which poses a significant challenge for sentiment analysis models. Traditional machine learning models are hindered by code-switching and can't effectively handle multilingual data due to issues like data imbalance and label bias. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a contrastive loss function, paired with a language identification module and an attention-based neural network architecture, to efficiently extract sentiment from tweets that contain code-switching. This method is compared to a baseline model, demonstrating improved performance and accuracy (-2.2% absolute improvement) when applied to the CST-14 dataset for tweets in Spanish and English.

We investigate a three-loop seesaw model of neutrino mass, which predicts a Majorana dark matter particle under specific conditions. This model is characterized by two distinct flavor structures - one resembling the standard model and the other resembling inverse hierarchy. Our study focuses on two types of dark matter candidates - a singlet scalar and a fermion - and examines their mass ranges in relation to various constraints. The results suggest that the dark matter particle can be either relatively heavy, exceeding 100 GeV, or relatively light, less than 20 GeV. Specifically, for the standard model flavor structure, a dark matter particle with a mass between 20-100 GeV is feasible, which is a range that could be confirmed by the KATRIN experiment. Conversely, for the inverse hierarchy structure, a dark matter particle with a mass between 40-120 GeV is also possible. In both cases, the dark matter particle would be more stable due to a small suppression from the standard model.

The Product-based Neural Network (PNN) is a cutting-edge machine learning model known for its exceptional performance in various tasks such as natural language processing and recommendation systems. PNNs comprise a unique architecture that effectively combines the interactions between different categorical features. However, the current PNN designs lack a clear understanding of cross-field interactions. To address this limitation, we developed an innovative PNN architecture called the CrossPNN, which enables the learning of cross-field interactions in a more explicit and efficient way. By treating the cross-field interactions as a new input field, the CrossPNN can better capture the complex relationships between different feature fields. Additionally, we designed a novel CrossPNN module that utilizes a multi-head attention mechanism to model the cross-field interactions, leading to improved representation learning and better performance. Experimental results across various datasets and applications confirm the effectiveness of the proposed CrossPNN approach.

This research focuses on the active role of intelligent reflecting surfaces in wireless networks, examining how channel state information is communicated between nodes to achieve optimal energy efficiency through beamforming. The study examines the impact of two distinct models on energy efficiency in active CSI sharing, incorporating CSI measurement errors and quantization effects. The study proves that equal weight is given to individual user and system performance in a unique fairness-energy efficiency trade-off. The study then proposes a novel algorithm, the Riemannian Proximal ADMM, to optimize beamforming with quantized CSI, and demonstrates its performance in active CSI sharing with quantized effects outperforming other methods in simulations.

The effectiveness of prediction in branch prediction operations is well-documented.
While traditional methods have been widely used, advances in deep learning techniques have led to the development of dynamic branch predictors capable of surpassing classical models.
This paper delves into the integration of a deep learning-based dynamic branch predictor with a countermeasures system, specifically focusing on the impact of countermeasures on the performance of a deep learning-based branch predictor.

This work introduces a camera control system known as AutoCam, enabling seamless monitoring and tracking of moving targets using an embedded camera. By combining the capabilities of a deep convolutional neural network with image processing techniques, AutoCam achieves accurate target following, even on unpredictable surfaces, and adapts to changes in its environment. Compared to traditional servo-based systems, AutoCam offers improved accuracy, robustness, and real-time response. Furthermore, AutoCam's camera positioning and target monitoring capabilities are demonstrated through various applications, including visual servoing, object tracking, and image segmentation.

We investigate the SOS (Simple exclusion process) model with external fields and stochastic boundary conditions under a finite volume and the zero external field condition. We find that, within the SOS model, there exist boundary laws which cannot be normalised normally, exhibiting complex phase transitions due to the presence of a non-normalisable boundary measure. This discovery expands on the SOS model's previously known phase transition phenomena, initially observed in the zero external field case with normalisable boundary measures. Our result is equivalent to demonstrating the existence of boundary laws exhibiting complex phase transitions in the Ising model with external fields and stochastic boundary conditions under finite volume and the zero external field condition.

Theoretical models of photon emission are developed for a specific type of light transfer, where two photons from an excited state return to their ground state. These models, which are based on a mathematical approach called the two-level model, predict the amount of light emitted and how it changes over time. Comparing these predictions to experimental data from a specific material reveals that the amount of light emitted at a specific energy level is significantly reduced when considering the excitation of other energy levels. This is attributed to the complex interplay of energy transfer pathways, which are typically not accounted for in simple models. As a result, the amount of light emitted at a specific energy level is no longer a reliable indicator of the excitation of a specific energy sublevel.

We use the light-cone QCD sum rules approach to calculate the strong coupling constants for hadron weak currents within the standard model's effective Hamiltonian. Our method involves constructing three-pion vector and scalar form factors, and then applying the finite energy sum rules method to extract the coupling constants. The results show reasonable agreement with existing estimates obtained through other methods.

Recent neutrino oscillation experiment results have garnered significant attention due to their alignment with several key anomalies: three small mixing angles, an anomaly-related mass difference, an unusual phase, and the large mass hierarchy discrepancy. We propose a unified, four-neutrino model incorporating the $\Delta \chi^2$ from the six short-baseline experiments, demonstrating that these anomalies are interdependent. Specifically, the $3+1$ oscillation model effectively explains the electron antineutrino anomaly when coupled with the $2+2$ model, which then resolves the muon neutrino anomaly, while the $\theta_{13}$ anomaly is addressed by the large-scale oscillation within the $\theta_{23}$ parameter. Furthermore, the unusual $3\sigma$ region of the $\Delta \chi^2$ profile corresponds to a mass hierarchy discrepancy, which is consistent with normal ordering, and the $\chi^2$ value can be significantly reduced by incorporating a fourth sterile neutrino.

In causal inference using observational data, the outcome and covariates are often weighted using a linear regression model. This has led to the development of methods that balance weights on arbitrary covariates, under the assumption that they closely match the 'balance scores' derived from experimental studies. We propose an approach that turns this assumption on its head: by employing an empirical process calculus, we first derive optimal balance scores for an imaginary experimental study, then utilize these scores as reference points to select weights for observational studies. This two-step process yields a sample size requirement for observational research, calibrated to yield the same power as its experimental counterpart. We also establish that, when the covariates are continuous, our approach produces semi-parametric efficient estimates, even in the presence of non-covariate adjustment. We support our findings with empirical evidence and simulation studies.

In modern power grids, voltage source converters play a crucial role in controlling local voltage levels. To effectively regulate these levels, their droop parameters must be adjusted correctly. This paper focuses on synchronizing and identifying the droop parameters of multiple generators connected to an infinite power supply. We introduce a control strategy that ensures stable operation within a specified time period, despite the presence of nonlinear characteristics and unknown conditions. To validate our approach, simulation results are provided.

We investigate the change in the type of light emitted by a collection of atoms undergoing a two-part atomic decay process. In this scenario, the light emitted consists of a single photon at a time, contrasting with the continuous, coherent light typically produced by one-atom decay. Notably, our findings suggest that the phase of the light's intensity can evolve over time, potentially giving rise to interesting optical properties, such as interference patterns, which could be harnessed for novel applications in quantum information science.

The metastability of kinks containing internal degrees of freedom is studied with a focus on how their classical manifestation occurs through the interaction of normal modes.  This mode-mediated interaction is responsible for the degradation of the system's stability.  A parameter-free model of the metastable kink is developed to quantify this effect.  We also explore how the interaction of collective internal and normal modes contributes to the degradation of kink stability, finding a correlation between this interaction and the kink's energy.  Collective modes' impact is most pronounced at low energies of the kink.  We also investigate how the potential used in a study can affect the kink's energy.  A comparison between the kink and the vortex reveals that the kink's energy is more susceptible to the potential used in the system.  We also find that the kink's energy is more sensitive to the potential used in the system when internal modes are included.  We also explore how the system's symmetries affect the kink's energy.  We also explore how the system's symmetries affect the degradation of the system's stability.  We also find that the kink's energy is more sensitive to the symmetries of the system.  We also find that the kink's energy is more sensitive to the symmetries of the system when internal modes are included.
