Utilizing algebraic and algebraic methods, we find and describe a singular, non-split $\U_q$ module with a dimension of 24 that does not fit within a known category and cannot be treated as a direct sum of modules. Moreover, we find and describe all the low-point weight subspaces within this 24-dimensional $\U_q$ module and calculate the corresponding multiplicities.

A mathematical model is developed to describe the growth of spherical grains in a two-phase system with anisotropic grains present in one phase. Building on previous work, a new equation is proposed that accounts for the growth of minor-phase grains and demonstrates how the introduction of the volume fraction of the major phase affects grain growth. It is shown that at high volume fractions the grain growth in a multiphase system converges to that of a single-phase system, and that grain-growth rates can be represented by an effective exponents. This effective exponent is found to depend on the mass ratio of the minor to major phase and is reduced at high volume fractions of the major phase. Furthermore, it is found that the grain-growth rate in a multiphase system is reduced at high volume fractions of the major phase, and that the grain-growth rate in a multiphase system is reduced at high volume fractions of the major phase.

We examine the effectiveness of contemporary human mesh recovery methods when given various dataset attributes that account for the challenges of generalizing to unknown subjects, poses, and expressions. A comprehensive, publicly available dataset is presented, comprising a substantial number of subjects, poses, and expressions, gathered from the internet and annotated through crowdsourcing. Our analysis involves a series of controlled experiments, in which we provide the HMR methods with different combinations of dataset attributes and evaluate their performance. The findings reveal that the attributes affect the methods' performance in distinct ways and that the attributes used by one method may be detrimental to another. Additionally, we provide the HMR methods with additional information, including the pose and expression labels, and utilize it to improve the generalization of their predictions. Our comprehensive study provides a thorough understanding of the effects of the dataset attributes on contemporary HMR methods and lays the groundwork for further research on this topic. The dataset and code used in our study can be found on our repository.

Within the Abrikosov-Larkin model, we calculate the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$ and its variation with electron interaction strength $V$, as well as the critical magnetic field $H_c$ for a system governed by the Anderson impurity model. Our analysis reveals a direct linear relationship between $T_c$ and $H_c$ for strong coupling, as well as a characteristic magnetic field saturation at a specific scale. Moreover, we observe a linear relationship between $T_c$ and $V$ for weakly coupled systems. Notably, we also identify a transition point where $T_c$ and $H_c$ shift to higher values, corresponding to a transition from Abrikosov-Larkin to BCS-like behavior.

In a five-dimensional brane model, we investigate the matching of effective field theory with the Standard Model at high energies to a five-dimensional model featuring Standard Model fields confined to the UV boundary, and new physics in a bulk region, whose effects are described by dimension-six operators. We then isolate the subset of dimension-six operators that gives rise to a Coleman-Weinberg brane instanton effect, and demonstrate that this setup yields a physically meaningful six-dimensional theory with a generalised $\phi^4$ potential.

This thesis aims to present an algorithmic and probabilistic machine learning technique that can be applied in the fields of medical image analysis, environmental prediction, and economic forecasting, utilizing techniques such as gradient-based learning and Bayesian inference, and exploring the possibilities of deep learning and sparse learning methodologies. The thesis focuses on developing an efficient sparse learning algorithm and a Bayesian deep learning approach, as well as investigating deep learning applications in image analysis, forecasting, and time series modeling.

A well-known terminal sliding mode control method is closely related to the
optimal switching issue, aiming to reduce settling time. In this research, a
 novel approach is applied to create a robust TSM control framework that achieves
the minimum settling time. The proposed strategy involves initially splitting the
settlement process into two stages using the established polytrack approach,
and then incorporating a switching function to dynamically select the most
effective path for settlement. The proposed scheme ensures the stability of the
closed-loop system and successfully minimizes the settling time. The
performance of the new control method is compared to other robust TSM control
schemes through a simulation of a two-degree-of-freedom single joint mechanical
arm.

The quality control of lithium-ion batteries can greatly benefit from the application of ultrasonic resonance techniques, especially in the large-scale manufacturing process where non-destructive examination is required in real-time. To support this, a simple, yet efficient method has been developed to calculate the elastic constants of Li-ion positive electrodes using ultrasonic resonance data. The positive electrodes were created with a thickness of 200 microns and produced in a square shape. To facilitate the calculation, a formula was derived to convert ultrasonic velocity measurements to elastic constants. The positive electrodes were examined using three different thickness settings, each with a 2 mm, 50 mm, and 100 mm, and measured using a bulk and surface wave technique. The calculated Poisson's ratio was also obtained through the application of the ultrasonic data, demonstrating a strong correlation with the results obtained from the electrochemical cycling process. The findings of this study will serve as a valuable tool in the ultrasonic quality control of Li-ion batteries, providing a means to assess the elastic properties of the positive electrodes during large-scale manufacturing.

This research focuses on the challenge of creating a flatness-based controller for discrete-time systems, which can be complex to define a suitable parametrizing map. We investigate the connection between discrete-time and continuous-time systems, highlighting the distinctness of the former. We introduce a novel category of discrete-time systems that share similarities with their continuous-time counterparts. This connection is utilized to develop a unified approach to flatness-based controller design, which is demonstrated through its application on specific models.

Our research involves developing a method to leverage curated datasets in 
conjunction with vast web-based data for image description generation.
Curated datasets like MSCOCO and Flickr30k provide high-quality image 
description data but are limited in quantity, whereas web-based data such as 
Concept-Activation Maps (CAM) contains a greater variety of image descriptions 
but are often lower in quality. To address this, we created a technique to 
integrate these datasets based on their respective qualities and then use 
supervised training to refine the output. Next, we use unsupervised learning to 
integrate the combined dataset with web-based data. Our results indicate that 
this approach results in more accurate image descriptions compared to a single 
dataset.

We establish that if $s_1,...,s_t$ are distinct strings from an alphabet of size $\sigma$, the maximum count of disjoint $k$-letter substrings $s_1,...,s_t$ that remain connected when one string is removed, depends logarithmically on the product of $k$ and $\sigma$. Furthermore, we prove this upper limit is absolute and only depends on $\sigma$ and $k$, when considering the maximum count of disjoint $k$-letter substrings whose removal results in a string that lacks a path. Additionally, we prove an absolute lower limit on the size of such a set of substrings that lack a path, which is related to the size of a largest independent set in a graph constructed from the substrings.

The article continues to explore ordered semigroups that can be structured as partial algebras equipped with a band of partial homomorphisms. This leads to a detailed analysis of two key types of semigroups within this framework: those with restricted right or left operations, and those with restricted two-sided operations. The study also connects these semigroups to variations of restricted semigroups and partial semigroups with a linear order.

The self-attention (SA) mechanism, a key component in numerous current top-performing deep models, is hindered by its substantial computational requirements due to a specific computational complexity of O(N^2). SA layers with a large number of heads and unreasonably high embedding sizes cause this inefficiency, prompting a re-evaluation of these design choices. Our research reveals that the optimal width for a highly parameterized self-attention network, with one million parameters, is 512. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the width of self-attention layers can be reduced to 256 (or even 128) without compromising performance by utilizing the fast Fourier transform (FFT). Utilizing FFT results in a unique scaling law for the model, allowing for more efficient training of extremely large datasets using fewer parameters.

BIO3 nanoparticles with varying sizes and phase types were created through a simple hydrothermal process, and their unique optical and magnetic properties were examined in-depth. Our analysis using spectroscopic ellipsometry revealed that the nanoparticles exhibited different band gap energies than their bulk counterpart, with both phase types displaying reduced band gaps relative to their bulk counterparts, although the rhombohedral phase showed a more significant band gap reduction. Moreover, the nanoparticles exhibited an enhanced absorption in the visible range compared to the bulk material, with the orthorhombohedral phase showing the strongest light absorption. Our results also showed that the nanoparticles retained their room temperature ferromagnetic property, with the orthorhombohedral phase exhibiting a more pronounced magnetic behavior. Our findings demonstrate the potential of these nanoparticles to potentially harness solar energy.

A detailed examination of the extended $331$ model is conducted to establish the theoretical foundations for the mass causes of the bottom quark and tau lepton, as well as other fermions. Through the application of a specific group theory, which incorporates the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries, and utilizing a representation of $SU(3)$, we identify specific mass generation mechanisms. These mechanisms involve the diagonalization of mass matrices in the extended $331$ model, which are further broken down by the effects of neutral and charged currents in the first generation of fermions. Additionally, this research proposes a new method for generating mass for the neutrinos through a combination of radiative and Majorana mechanisms.

Learning the shapes of objects grasped in images of human actions is a complex task, especially when the objects in question have intricate and hard to describe appearances. We present a novel approach to learning the shapes of opaque objects grasped in images. This approach consists of two main components: (1) a signed distance function that represents the 3D shape of an object by mapping points to their proximity to the object's surface, and (2) an implicit network that estimates this distance based on the object's image observations. Our proposed method outperforms existing techniques by incorporating a robust feature representation based on the Grayscale Moment Invariant Norm, which is particularly effective in handling occlusions and lighting variations. Furthermore, we introduce a synthetic data generation method that effectively simulates real-world occlusions and lighting changes, which significantly enhances the model's performance when trained with this data. Our method's efficacy is validated by superior performance on the Cornell Grasp and Yale Grasp datasets in terms of accuracy and robustness.

The development of advanced solar mission capabilities in the 2020s has created opportunities to study long-term changes in the chromosphere, specifically using the Solar Orbiter+ESA's coronagraph. This requires the ability to analyze data from multiple solar mission archives and compare it with data from future missions. We have therefore designed a new method, Equal Contrast, which enables the production of a standardized, spatially-resolved time series from diverse datasets with different spatial resolutions, using a combination of mathematical algorithms and data analysis techniques. This methodology enables the aggregation of multiple datasets into a single, continuous time series, specifically addressing the challenges posed by low-resolution data from the chromosphere. We have tested Equal Contrast using simulated data from a range of spatial resolutions, and have found that it effectively preserves the original characteristics of the data, including variations in intensity, shape, and overall structure. This new methodology will be a valuable tool in the analysis of upcoming solar mission data, and is set to be applied in a future study using the Solar Orbiter+ESA data.

The LHCb experiment is conducting a search for a new type of particle formation when a Sigma-plus particle breaks down into a Lambda and a positive pion, using a vast dataset of proton-proton collisions recorded at 7, 8, and 13 TeV energy levels. The experiment has found no evidence to suggest the existence of new particles beyond those predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics.

In parallel symbolic execution, splitting up the work based on test depth offers flexibility in choosing search strategies. However, managing this process among multiple workers can be inefficient when they rely on sharing intermediate results, leading to slow convergence. Our solution is a new approach called Test-Depth Partitioning with Synchronization (TDPS), which makes it easy to parallelize symbolic execution while keeping execution costs low. By using a single global test depth counter, TDPS ensures that workers don't share intermediate results, allowing them to quickly switch to a new test depth counter when converging search strategies change. Our experimental results show that TDPS is 1.4-3.3 times faster than existing methods for finding vulnerabilities in real-world programs, and is also more robust to changes in search strategies. Our approach has been made available as an extension to the AEGIS parallel execution tool.

The magnetic properties of an ensemble of nanoparticles with anisotropic moments are studied under various external magnetic field conditions.  The results indicate that the rate of magnetization dissipation in these systems is maximized when the external field is parallel to the nanocrystals' orientation axis, and minimal when perpendicular to it.  These findings suggest that the magnetic response of a nanocrystal suspension is influenced by the distribution of the anisotropy axis among the individual particles.  The magnetic relaxation response of a nanocrystal suspension can be used to gain insights into its microstructural organization.

Federated learning is a rapidly evolving area in machine learning that enables collaborative model training across a network of edge devices without central oversight, which is highly appealing for applications requiring secure data privacy and reduced device data transmission. However, this approach is hindered by the need for a central server to manage model updates, which becomes impractical in settings without such a central entity. This limitation is addressed by Online Push-Sum (OPS), a novel method enabling federated learning in a decentralized manner within a network of devices without a central server. By utilizing OPS, devices can locally train models, then transmit aggregated model updates to other devices for further training, allowing devices to become model trainers or data sources. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of OPS in achieving accurate model training while minimizing data transmission.

Predicting dialog acts on the fly is a crucial task for conversational agents, yet most existing models focus solely on the current turn, disregarding prior conversations. To address this, we introduce a novel approach where a recurrent neural network is trained to utilize preceding short texts as input, enhancing the model with a context-aware attention mechanism. Our method is adaptable to various short text representations, and we evaluate it on the DSTC3 dataset, achieving comparable results with the winning submission. Notably, our model's performance improves significantly when incorporating non-trivial short texts, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing contextual information and suggesting that it can also enhance models in other conversation prediction tasks by leveraging summarization or user history.

We've developed a comprehensive comparison study on the performance differences of telecentric etalon-based instruments, which are a type of high-resolution spectrograph. By modeling these instruments in different configurations, we found that telecentronic instruments offer significant advantages. This is because their focal length properties allow for a notable speed increase of approximately two times, achieved by having a focal length within the instrument's beam that matches the etalon's length. As a result, telecentronic instruments can be designed with shorter focal lengths, smaller size, lower weight, higher stability, and lower susceptibility to misalignment. Furthermore, we observed that telecentronic instruments exhibit lower sensitivity to both axial and lateral lens misalignment. Notably, we found that telecentronic instruments exhibit an exceptionally low sensitivity to lateral lens misalignment, with a change in wavelength of less than 0.1 nm per millimeter of misalignment.

In the context of graph theory, labeling a set of points in the plane with n points and real numbers can be regarded as a linear extension of these numbers. A set of points is compatible with a simple graph G if each pair of numbers corresponding to adjacent vertices in G are close in value. The theory of graph labeling explores the characteristics of these compatible pairs. We demonstrate that in any set of n points with n being sufficiently large, any subset consisting of at least 2n/ln(n) points allows a single-edge compatible matching but no other matching with 2n/ln(n) edges. Furthermore, labeling with n points with n being sufficiently large requires at least (1-1/ln(n))n copies of any set of points for a single-edge compatible matching.

This research outlines a software development platform called ChipletC. It enables users to create software programs that can run efficiently on specialized chiplet-based hardware designs. An innovative software concept called Codelet is proposed, which represents a program executed on chiplets in a similar manner to threads. Our demonstration of ChipletC involves a hypothetical scenario of creating software for a reconfigurable financial trading device, which uses ChipletC to facilitate creation, verification, and synthesis of chiplets and Codelet programs.

A recent study in survival analysis with a large number of covariates has employed the presmoothing technique to improve estimator accuracy. The method involves initially estimating the proportional hazards model via maximum likelihood, then using these estimates to fit a secondary model. The method is analogous to two-stage estimation, yet maximizes the hazard rate and not just the distribution. The study demonstrates the convergence rate of this estimator to be the same as that of maximum likelihood estimation after adjusting for truncation at the end. The study further shows that presmoothing can be viewed as a form of double robustness. The method has been found to perform well in simulation studies and in practical applications such as studying kidney failure treatment.

The focus of this research lies in exploring the nonlocal metric dimension of specific graphs, namely, lexicographic, cartography, join, join of disjoint cliques, clique, comb, bipartite graph, and strong product graphs. The study yields the following findings. First, certain lexicographic and strong product graph classifications emerge based on their topological invariants. Additionally, specific strong product graphs are identified as having a nonlocal metric dimension of 1. Moreover, particular strong product graphs with a nonlocal metric dimension of n(G) - 2 are presented. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive description of strong product graphs with a nonlocal metric dimension of 2. Moreover, exact nonlocal metric dimension values are determined for cartography, join, join of disjoint cliques, and strong product graphs. Finally, the study outlines necessary conditions for the nonlocal metric dimension of a strong product graph to equal n(G), equal to n(G) - 1, or 2.

This paper presents a novel method for automatically identifying and exploiting the side-channel attack surface of deep learning frameworks, specifically designed to target measurements such as power traces. By leveraging the application of side-channel attacks to deep learning, the proposed system identifies the most vulnerable entry points in the architecture using a combination of search-based optimization and a side-channel attack algorithm. Once potential vulnerabilities are identified, the attack algorithm is refined through a meta-heuristic optimization process to ensure it effectively targets the key entry points. Our approach is demonstrated through a comprehensive case study, successfully executing a precise zero-out attack against the MNIST dataset using the well-known COT attack algorithm against a Convolutional Neural Network, disabling over 90% of specific neurons within the network.

To reduce the length of polarization fibers, we use two statistical methods. 
First, we establish confidence limits for partial distances within three specific fiber designs: D, F, and C. 
These limits enable the design of optimized fibers with reduced lengths compared to their original counterparts. 
Building on this approach, we develop a second method centered around designing fibers with precise path lengths for specific designs, such as D, F, C, and P. 
By randomly sampling from a Gaussian distribution, we establish precise length-based bounds around the mean length of optimized fibers. 
Ultimately, we combine these statistical methods to design compact polarization fibers with precise axial orientations (PAs) and low bending sensitivity, suitable for compact imaging systems that require high numerical apertures.

A new method for self-supervised 2D denoising in seismic time-series analysis has been developed. The approach involves three stages: data preparation, training, and signal processing. In the initial stage, data is cleaned up through a denoising process, and a synthetic dataset is created using the filtered data to serve as training examples. The second stage involves creating self-supervised training examples from the synthetic data by applying various time-series denoising techniques without explicit ground truth information. The third stage involves using these self-trained examples to automatically denoise real-world seismic data. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in enhancing signal quality and identifying subsurface structures. Furthermore, a comprehensive evaluation was conducted to assess the performance of the self-trained models, and the findings indicate that the initial data cleaning step significantly improves the self-supervised training process.

A theoretical model has been developed to analyze real photon emission in lepton scattering, with a focus on how this process impacts charge asymmetry measurements. Initial calculations, conducted within the Born approximation and an effective field theory framework, suggest that photon emission has a sub-dominant effect on the observed charge asymmetry. Notably, this impact is more pronounced when considering broader kinematical thresholds for the particle decays. Our analysis indicates that, at a thermal equilibrium state, where lepton momentum is approximately 1 GeV, the photon correction to the asymmetry is negative and lies in the range of -0.1 to -0.2%.

Theoretical models of Mott insulators created by chemical or physical methods suggest that their electronic structures are influenced by spin-polaronic ladders, which in turn affect their electronic properties and interactions. In this research, we examine the effects of spin-polaronic ladders on the Fermi surface of 3D metals, discovering that these ladders can cause a breakdown of the Fermi surface into isolated islands, even in the absence of long-range interactions. Our findings are discussed within the context of recent experiments on MnSi.

We've developed a novel estimator for continuous treatments that remains robust in the presence of unmeasured confounding variables, which is based on the concept of optimal treatment regimes. Our method, which relies on local polynomial regression, enables the estimation of optimal treatment parameters. To ensure the reliability of our findings, we conduct a simulation study to assess the performance of our estimator. Furthermore, we utilize the estimator to analyze a real-world dataset, which involves examining the relationship between left ventricular diastolic function and right heart pressure in patients with pulmonary hypertension, leveraging data from the UK Research GEM trial. Our findings have significant implications for policy-making and policy-evaluation in randomized controlled trials.

Recent research on starshades has gained momentum due to advanced star image destruction technology, benefiting both the study of exoplanets and extreme astronomy. This study combines existing research on starshades to provide a unified framework that can guide future studies, considering factors like telescope limitations, observation time, and data quality. By integrating recent starshade experiments, this paper aims to create a cohesive understanding of starshades, making it a valuable resource for researchers. By leveraging the collective knowledge from various experiments, this paper demonstrates the potential for collective understanding and presents a valuable reference for future starshade studies.

Previous datasets used for identifying suicidal texts online have significant limitations, primarily due to their small size and restricted annotation scope. The use of natural language processing techniques relies heavily on this annotation. To address this issue, we have developed the Robin dataset, which includes 11,000 text samples and 10% detailed annotations. The dataset covers a broader range of sources, including social media and online forums. The annotation process in Robin incorporates additional layers of information and support from mental health professionals, thereby improving on previous efforts. The experiments conducted demonstrate that data-driven models can perform competitively with models that heavily rely on pre-defined categories. Furthermore, Robin's annotations enable the development of more effective content-based models. The dataset is expected to significantly contribute to the advancement of automatic text-based suicidal crisis detection.

A novel approach to constructing supersymmetric versions of the Schwarzian action is introduced through a reduction method. This reduction is achieved by applying supersymmetric principles to a previously known action, constrained by $N$ fermionic symmetries and with a specific type of space-dependent central charge within its original symmetry algebra. The resulting super-Schwarzian action then emerges from this constrained reduction, which yields constraints on the super-Schwarzian function and resulting supersymmetric actions. This framework enables the derivation of multiple known and novel supersymmetric Schwarzian actions, including a version with $N=1$ that naturally leads to the most straightforward mechanism for generating holographic two-point functions, a key feature of holographic CFTs.

This work combines elements from dynamical systems, algebraic geometry, and number theory, with a focus on dynamical aspects of rational and polynomial maps, as well as equations.  The research presented here was carried out over several years, including during author's involvement with the Canadian Mathematical Society's General Mathematical and Applied and Industrial Mathematics Topical Group.  The research's outcomes have potential implications in fields including signal processing, optics and physics.

This paper explores the properties of electrically charged black holes set within anti-de Sitter space, and shows that such solutions to Einstein's equations naturally stem from a specific class of nonlinear electrodynamics within a four-dimensional space. Building on a previously introduced framework, we find that these solutions can be seen as the GR limit of a broader class of gauge and gravitational theories that incorporate certain types of p-form fields.

We examine the question of whether infinite Sidon sets exist for linear combinations
of the natural numbers, given a set of real coefficients. This problem has previously
been solved for real coefficients and partially solved for integer coefficients. Our
research builds on previous findings and partially resolves the problem for complex
coefficients, specifically showing that an infinite Sidon set can be found for any
linear combination of complex coefficients, provided at least one coefficient is not a
non-real integer. Additionally, our study includes specific cases where an infinite Sidon
set can be found and has implications for a conjecture in number theory regarding the
existence of primes in arithmetic progressions.

A connection between the geometric phase induced by an adiabatic process and the magnetic susceptibility at a quantum phase transition is theoretically investigated.  The adiabatic process in this investigation occurs when a slowly changing external transverse magnetic field interacts with a non-relativistic spin-1/2 particle within a time-dependent non-degenerate energy state.  We derive a general formula for the susceptibility in terms of the adiabatic curvature and show how susceptibility can be measured experimentally by tracking the change in the quantum state associated with the energy level as the magnetic field is varied, providing a direct link between the magnetic response and the geometric properties of the system.

Infinite fluctuations can significantly impact the behavior of ferromagnetic systems as they cool and reach critical temperatures. By simulating Monte Carlo methods, we investigate these critical fluctuations in a two-dimensional Ising model and its three- and four-dimensional counterparts. Our research demonstrates that by slowing down the cooling process, the system's final magnetic moment converges towards its critical value. Additionally, we examine the critical slowing down phenomenon and develop a theoretical model to describe it. This theoretical framework effectively predicts the critical temperature shift in two-dimensional Ising systems and three-dimensional ferromagnetic transition.

Recent studies on quasicrystals have identified a significant phenomenon where bound states arise due to the interaction between quasiperiodic potentials and the underlying crystal structure. This transition is known to be influenced by the way potential units are arranged within quasiperiodic structures. Through numerical analysis of a simplified model, we have investigated how this arrangement affects the characteristics of these bound states, specifically examining variations in band structure, localization properties, and spectral properties. Our findings have revealed that these properties are highly responsive to the specific quasiperiodic arrangement and can even change in abrupt, quantifiable ways.

Task-oriented dialogue systems in multiple languages typically rely on limited, machine-translated data which is often inaccurate and leads to conflicting outputs when generated from different sources. To address this issue, we introduce a method that leverages joint language model pre-training on monolingual dialogues in each language and subsequently fine-tune it on a small, multilingual dataset. Notably, pre-training on extensive dialogue datasets enhances the model's ability to encode the complex structure of conversations, significantly improving its performance in few-shot learning scenarios. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on a range of benchmarks across seven languages, outperforming existing systems in terms of effectiveness and significantly reducing the need for expensive human-annotated data.

Single-cell RNA-seq has been instrumental in understanding gene expression over time in living organisms by providing a detailed, single-cell resolution. This research focuses on a longitudinal analysis of RNA-seq time series data to uncover the differential expression and splicing patterns, with a goal of accurately modeling the data through a probabilistic framework. The model, known as the RNA-seq model, views the data as a non-negative count process and utilizes a Dirichlet process mixture to represent the hidden components. The model's parameters are estimated using a nonparametric maximum likelihood method, which involves a method selection approach to determine the number of components in the mixture. This approach is then compared with other methods, such as a Dirichlet process mixture with a prior on the mixture components, and a Bayesian nonparametric approach that assumes a finite mixture with a growing number of components. The comparison shows that the RNA-seq model offers a more accurate and efficient method for analyzing RNA-seq time series data.

We've developed a new approach to help engineers design technical measures that meet the requirements outlined in standard data protection impact assessments, thereby bridging the gap between legal and technical experts and reducing potential privacy breaches. Our solution involves a collaborative process where high-school students, paired with law students working on real-life cases, engage in a simulated activity where they design software features and receive feedback from legal experts on their compliance with data protection regulations. We evaluated our method through a comparative study, assessing its effectiveness in producing compliant features and privacy-respecting designs, and found that it outperforms traditional design methods by enhancing the interaction between students from the legal and technical disciplines, thereby increasing efficiency and reducing potential privacy breaches.

We develop the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework to compute the higher-order azimuthal cumulants for multiplicity distributions of charged particles in heavy-ion collisions, accounting for both initial gluon condensate fluctuations and coordinate transformations within the framework. This analysis reveals the distinct impacts of the system's initial fluctuations and coordinate evolution. Furthermore, our prediction that the higher-order azimuthal cumulants exhibit negative values at small final net charge (Q) values is supported by both ALICE's data for Q = 0 and model-predicted results for CGC-LHC, demonstrating significant correlation between charged particles in small Q events.

Theoretical models are used to analyze how light nuclei (deuterons, helions, and alpha particles) are produced in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, taking into account both thermal production and the breaking apart of smaller particles. By using three different approaches to describe this process, researchers examine how the results vary with different assumptions and find that the production of larger nuclei is most affected when assuming that these nuclei are formed from larger particles. Calculations show that thermal production is not significant at high collision energies and that the study of lighter nuclei (such as deuterons) can help researchers understand how they are produced. Furthermore, researchers have calculated the ratios of certain heavier nuclei (like helium-3 and helium-4) and found them to be consistent with data from the Particle Data Book. Finally, researchers have used their models to predict how the production of these nuclei will change with different collision energies and rapidity.

The discovery of multiple planets within the habitable zone of nearby stars, such as the TRAPPIST-1 system, has significantly contributed to our understanding of their formation and evolution. By studying exoplanets and their host stars, we can gain insights into the processes that shaped the planetary material and, in turn, the atmospheric properties of these worlds. The atmospheric properties of exoplanets are crucial in determining the presence of liquid water on their surfaces, a key factor in their potential to support life. The composition of a planet's atmosphere is primarily determined by its parent star's characteristics, including temperature, metallicity, and elemental patterns. The unique chemical features of exoplanets offer a direct link to their host stars, with variations often resulting from distinct stellar environments. The analysis of atmospheric gases in exoplanets and their implications for life on these planets will be discussed, with a particular focus on the TRAPPIST-1 system and its intriguing similarities and contrasts with other planets found around M-type stars.

This work investigates the dispersal of functions on specific types of circulant graphs, focusing on those with a jump length of three or less. It initially outlines the essential characteristics of these graphs, before employing advanced mathematical techniques to derive precise, tight-lower bound estimates for dispersal on various regular circulant graphs, including those with an odd number of vertices. Furthermore, we provide an exact analysis of dispersal on the circulant graph consisting of 8 vertices. Our study also extends to the complete circulant graph, where we establish the existence of highly dispersive functions and calculate lower bounds for dispersal on these graphs.

The Nested Neumann algorithm has demonstrated superior performance in solving monotone inclusions, particularly in terms of convergence speed, as it can solve 2-step problems in a single iteration. This improved performance can be attributed to a key insight, focusing on the inception depth - the layer at which the problem's complexity shifts, allowing the algorithm to leverage its enhanced capability. By doing so, the algorithm can bypass the need for repeated iterations, akin to bypassing roads with tolls. Building on this understanding, the algorithm's applicability has been extended to multiple other methods, such as the ADMM, FISTA, and PDHG, resulting in new variants with superior performance in solving specific types of problems. This development is particularly significant, as it offers a novel approach to addressing complex problems, while providing analytical justification for existing algorithms with improved step sizes, as well as insight into their potential for further optimization.

We investigated the impact of the cosmic friction term on the boost phenomenon in a single-field inflationary scenario. To do so, we employed a slow-roll single-field inflation model and analyzed the evolution of curvature perturbations during the inflationary era. We discovered that the cosmic friction term has a considerable influence on the boost, as revealed by the effective potential generated through non-linear mixing. This effect is significant and needs to be taken into account in future studies on the boost phenomenon, particularly in models involving multiple fields.

This study examines the effects of offering limited-flight fares on airline demand. According to the offered-come-at-you-as-you-are (OCATAYASY) hypothesis, introducing limited fares benefits airlines in two ways: it prevents the loss of existing customers and encourages more people to book and potentially increase total demand. However, this approach requires careful pricing to ensure it's effective. Using data from 2015 to 2017 and focusing on flights within the United States under 8 hours, I found that prices above $450 tend to limit demand, while prices below $300 can create additional demand and enhance overall demand. Additionally, I discovered that offering restricted fares to second-class flights increases demand more than doing so for first-class flights.

The casebase dataset and design have gained increasing recognition for offering valuable insights into the effectiveness of treatments in real-world settings. However, a widely accepted software tool to analyze such data has been lacking until now. Our research presents the casebase R package, a comprehensive set of tools for data analysis, visualization, and model creation. In a significant departure from earlier packages, casebase leverages the power of the glm function, a fundamental data analysis tool in R, allowing users to develop a wide range of models, including logistic, Cox, Poisson, and Gaussian models, tailored to continuous or binary outcomes. Additionally, we introduce a new function to calculate the size of a study and provide a function to generate simulated data for casebase designs. Our package includes numerous examples showcasing its capabilities, and we demonstrate its efficiency by comparing it to a commonly used package, survcomp. Through a series of simulations and casebase design examples, we demonstrate the casebase package's superiority in handling complex survival data and its ease of use, making it an ideal choice for clinical researchers.

A novel semi-numerical method has been developed for solving the Schrodinger equation, which uses an analytical solution to the differential equation derived from the Laplace transform of the differential operator. This semi-numerical approach is applied to the Coulomb potential and the $1/r^2$ potential, and the results from numerical calculations confirm that the method achieves an exceptional level of accuracy with minimal convergence iterations required, typically less than 5. Furthermore, the method has been extended to the Gross-Pitaevskii equation used to describe mean-field phenomena in bosonic many-body systems, and the key properties and stability of the analytical quasi-bound state are examined. This semi-numerical approach is expected to lead to more precise results in particle physics calculations.

The demand for high-performance, highly available distributed file systems is rising, particularly in fields like high-performance computing, data analytics, and cloud computing. In this paper, we examine a key design challenge for distributed file systems: scaling. The POSIX file system's hierarchical structure poses significant scalability limitations by leading to slow file name lookup times as the system grows. Existing solutions attempt to mitigate these limitations by expanding the file hierarchy in various ways, but these often come with their own drawbacks, including reduced performance and scalability. In contrast, object storage systems have a more natural hierarchical structure, making them better suited for high scalability. However, these systems typically sacrifice support for file and POSIX functionality. We propose a novel file system called WiserD, which combines the benefits of object storage systems with a hierarchical structure that is specifically tailored to files and the POSIX interface. The file system's architecture is designed to distribute both files and hierarchies across a hierarchical tree, while also leveraging the file hierarchy to manage files efficiently. The file system's architecture is also designed to distribute both files and hierarchies across a hierarchical tree, while also leveraging the file hierarchy to manage files efficiently. The file system's architecture is also designed to distribute metadata across a hierarchical tree, while also leveraging the file hierarchy to manage files efficiently. As electric vehicles (EVs) and parking facilities continue to rise, the demand for limited charging resources within these facilities has increased, leading to increased competition among users.  An effective way to manage this limited charging supply and ensure efficient use of resources is to implement a pricing mechanism.  This study focuses on the effectiveness of different online charging pricing methods in managing the charging process, particularly within parking facilities.  By comparing the performance of two online pricing mechanisms, the uniform pricing mechanism and the priority-based pricing mechanism, the research aims to understand how these methods impact charging resource allocation among users.  Through a comprehensive analysis of a simulation-based experiment, the results show that the priority-based pricing mechanism is more effective in releasing charging resources in real-time compared to the uniform pricing mechanism.  Furthermore, the results suggest that the priority-based pricing mechanism can be improved by adjusting its design parameters, allowing it to effectively manage the charging process, particularly in situations with high competition for charging resources.  This research contributes to the development of a more efficient charging management system that can improve the charging process, particularly in parking facilities.

We suggest innovative techniques for generating new, Hermitian Low-Density Parity Check (H-L-DPC) codes based on the existing narrow-sense MDS (NSMDS) code set. Utilizing these methods, we successfully construct multiple H-LDPC codes with diverse characteristics, specifically targeting the construction of H-LDPC codes suitable for use in free-distance maximization and minimizing row overlaps.

In a recent computation, we derived the integrals needed for scattering in Einstein gravity combined with a self-interacting scalar field at the next-to-next-to leading order. Our research involved deriving the next-to-next-to leading order scattering amplitudes for scalar particles in Einstein gravity using the compactified flat space approach. This was achieved by employing the compactified flat space approach up to a higher gauge degree, which allowed us to derive the next-to-next-to leading order amplitudes with significantly fewer required integrals - specifically, five integrals, compared to the six integrals needed at the next-to leading order in a different approach. Furthermore, we have extended our derivation to the next-to-next-to next-to leading order, achieving this by employing an iterative method to derive the next-to-next-to next-to leading order amplitudes from the next-to-next-to next-to leading order integrals.

The integration of variable renewable energy (RE) plays a vital role in transitioning away from fossil fuels and reducing carbon emissions. However, RE's expansion can lead to increased land use, potentially compromising short-term community assets and long-term goals. This research investigates land use-related consequences resulting from RE expansion on electricity costs, focusing on scenarios involving solar and wind power. Using detailed data and in-depth analysis, the study reveals that higher land use risks can significantly boost electricity costs, especially when relying heavily on solar power. However, the study also finds that limiting site choices for new sites can help mitigate land use-related costs and ensure affordable clean energy transitions. Notably, the relationship between land use risks and electricity costs is influenced by the distribution of RE capacity between solar and wind power. Ultimately, the study's findings provide valuable insights for decision-makers when balancing the need for clean energy with the need to minimize the strain on public land and community resources.

Cluster-randomized trials frequently employ the outcome measure's rate to assess treatment efficacy. For example, researchers examine the incidence of adverse events associated with COVID-19 vaccines by calculating the proportion of individuals infected within clusters receiving the vaccine or a control group without it. However, since vaccines often provide protection not only to those who receive it but also to those who did not, the impact of vaccination on individuals who didn't receive it is difficult to measure directly. We propose a method using generalized linear mixed models to estimate the within-cluster direct treatment effect under this framework. Additionally, we derive a formula for calculating the maximum expected effect, which can be used to determine the sample size for designing such trials. Our proposed method is applied in a real-world study examining the effectiveness of the BNT162b2 vaccine.

This paper proposes a method for calculating the multiplicative degree-$\kappa$ Kirchhoff index of layered directed graphs efficiently, where $\kappa$ is any nonnegative integer value. The method builds upon previous research, specifically a formula for calculating the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index of undirected graphs, to establish a theoretical framework for layered directed graphs. The method also leverages topological indices, specifically the degree-Kirchhoff index, to quantify the complexity of layered directed graphs and demonstrates its practical application.

We investigate contextual linear bandits where agents share knowledge about a context space $X$. By assuming that the distribution $D$ governing the context space is shared among all agents, we show that this shared knowledge reduces communication needs in a bandit setting. Specifically, we find that the minimum required communication bits to reach a desired level of regret is affected by the distribution $D$, resulting in lower communication costs in many scenarios. This generalizes existing results on private bandits and extends them to contextual settings with both discrete and continuous contexts.

To mitigate the negative impact of uneven class distributions on model performance, researchers have employed various methods such as undersampling major classes and oversampling minor classes.  However, oversampling methods often overlook the underlying data distribution and may even exacerbate the issue.  A more effective approach involves using generative models to generate synthetic data from minority classes, but this comes with its own challenges, such as ensuring generated data remains unbiased.  This paper presents an innovative oversampling method called UMBRO to address class imbalance by augmenting the minority class with undersampling the major class.  By doing so, it aims to reverse the effects of class imbalance, making the training data more representative of the actual distribution, and has been shown to improve model performance on imbalanced datasets.  UMBRO outperforms current methods by achieving better results on a range of benchmark datasets, and its source code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/saurabhsurana1/UMBRO.

The leading cause of errors in various measurements at colliders, including those related to the unitary-triangle angle gamma and CP violation in charm particles, often stems from the limited knowledge of particle decay amplitudes. Consequently, researchers are pursuing multi-body decays at the LHC to gauge precision. The collaboration behind the LHCb experiment, which has pioneered the study of three-body particle decays, is working to expand its research scope through upgraded equipment, including the High-Luminosity LHC and upgraded LHCb detector, both of which are expected to provide a 50 times increase in data availability. The innovative research presented here will play a vital role in advancing the field of study and facilitating future studies.

A substantial proportion of scientific publications involves statistical analysis, 
yielding insights for other research, informing policy decisions, or predicting future outcomes. To achieve higher reproducibility, researchers can utilize advanced methods, such as sharing underlying data and promoting transparency. Recent research has demonstrated the applicability of text mining to uncover hidden relationships in statistics, underscoring the importance of this field. By applying principles of evidence-based medicine, researchers can further enhance their work. This article examines the intersection of statistics and text mining, highlighting the benefits and limitations of integrating these disciplines to improve research resilience.

A cutting-edge technique for 'flying focus X' enables a single laser to cover an extensive range of work areas while maintaining a uniform focus diameter across the workspace. By integrating a two-axis zoom system into a goniometer, the system offers a high degree of flexibility and can be scaled up to meet specific needs. We detail a system design approach to address potential scaling issues, such as limited stroke, high-speed motion, and optical constraints. This architecture is specifically tailored for supporting high-resolution stereomicroscopy, digital image correlation, and other demanding applications.

The FIRA HuroCup league's humanoid robots have undergone a decade of competitive events, modeled after the RoboCup challenge. Established in 2005 as a virtual 2010 RoboCup, the competition evolved into a real-world RoboCup Humanoid Challenge for its sixth edition in 2011, mirroring the Olympic Games concept. The competition, now in its twelfth edition, has seen a significant increase in participation, especially from China, Korea, Japan, France and the US, producing substantial improvements in performance. The robots, required to navigate an outdoor environment, have successfully completed a challenging 5-stage obstacle course within 100 seconds, using a color camera to gather information, and have demonstrated the effectiveness of the HuroCup as a testbed for human-robot interaction applications.

To address cross-domain recommendation issues in social networks, we've developed a new, more efficient approach that integrates metric learning techniques to measure and compare the similarities between users and items across separate platforms. This method leverages the available text data from the networks to enhance its recommendation capabilities. By employing the metric learning framework, we can not only improve the accuracy of our system but also provide users with personalized item suggestions that are easy to understand by reducing the learned embeddings into a transparent representation. This enables users to understand why items are recommended to them. Our proposed model, called Leveraged Cross-Network Recommendation (LCNR), has been tested on real-world social networks and has shown promising results.

This study presents a new model of automata where two finite-state machines interact in a parallel manner and communicate through a stream of bits. To study this model's expressive capabilities, we consider automata with distinct transition systems and examine their capacity to recognize specific languages. By comparing these two models, we address long-standing unresolved issues related to their comparative expressive powers.

A new model has been proposed to account for heat transfer in two-dimensional complex plasma systems by incorporating detailed vibrational properties. This comprehensive vibrational model takes into account the effects of nearest and farther-nearest neighbor interactions, allowing for the derivation of a comprehensive expression for the vibrational density of states in two-dimensional systems. By applying the model to a specific case involving sodium chloride, the calculated transport properties are found to be in excellent agreement with experimentally measured values, demonstrating the model's utility in predicting transport properties in two-dimensional systems.

This paper introduces a novel constraint-based decision procedure for unordered Petri nets, built upon the use of counter machines with unordered data. By translating Petri net models into their counter machine counterparts, the paper demonstrates that certain Petri net configurations can express complex relationships that previously required more extensive data structures, such as lists. By developing a method to merge these data structures, the paper establishes a two-way conversion between the two models. Furthermore, the paper presents a decision-making algorithm for testing the possibility of net states, leveraging the conversion and a novel satisfiability-checking procedure for existential while-universal programs with data. This procedure is then applied to various Petri net problems, offering alternative approaches to multiple existing decision procedures. Experimental results confirm the procedure's effectiveness.

To create high frame rate (HFR) videos for coronary angiography from sequential, reduced frame rate (RF) videos, we have developed a new model. The goal of this work is to produce not only high-quality video, but also a 3D volume for coronary angiography. The proposed deep learning model is a modified version of the Recurrent Network (RN), which includes a convolutional network for generating a 3D volume and a temporal convolution network for video generation. The network architecture is flexible and allows for the use of pre-trained weights from the volume model with the video model. We have also developed a method to reduce the time required for computing HFR videos and a strategy for training the network using a large dataset. The results of our experiments demonstrate that the generated HFR videos and volumes perform better than those produced by other deep learning models and a motion compensation method. Specifically, the PSNR of our generated HFR videos was found to be significantly higher than that of the other deep learning models and the motion compensation method. The time required for computing our HFR videos was also significantly lower than that of the other deep learning models.

The precise topological analysis of numerous heavy particles' rare decays is crucial for assessing CKM unitarity. The ultra-low background conditions of the FCC-ee make it an ideal location for this type of measurement. The following report outlines the simulation of rare decays at FCC-ee, namely, the decay of D to K pi and the misidentification of B mesons as D mesons, as well as an initial topological analysis of D mesons. The report also includes a simulation of the D meson's decay into K star pi star, which is a challenging task due to the high rate of D star decays into a K star and a pi star, which can be mistaken for a D meson. The study also includes a detailed study of the B star to D star decay, as well as a preliminary study of the D+ meson's decay into K+ pi+, the latter of which is complicated by its similarity to the D+ to K+ K+ pi- decay patterns.

We have derived a theoretical framework for coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering and applied it to the conditions of dark matter direct detection experiments. This framework was found to be consistent with the experimental findings of 39 Ne by providing both quantitative and qualitative agreement. The proposed model also offers a potential explanation for the observed enhancement in multiple experiments and may account for the excess found in 76 Ge, which falls within the expected range. Utilizing this model, the sensitivity limits of 1800 and 600 GeV for spin-independent dark matter interactions with nucleons in 19 Ge and 7 GeV neutrino-nucleus scattering, respectively, have been determined for a 5.9 kg.yr exposure period that corresponds to the first detection of 7 GeV neutrinos.

The gravitational influence of a distant intermediate-mass companion hasaltered the orbits of stars near the central supermassive black hole,our analysis reveals. By drawing upon existing research on the dynamics ofsuch systems, we develop a simplified model that enables the calculationof the perturbation's strength. Utilizing this model, we investigate how theperturbation affects the observed motion of stars within the Sgr A*galactic center, a system where a two-year monitoring project has provided us with precise orbital data. Our findings show that the observed starorbits exhibit a pattern consistent with the predicted gravitationalinfluence of a 69 M$_{\odot}$ companion, located approximately 3000 AU from Sgr A*. This analysis yields a 3-sigma upper limit for the perturbation strength,which we use to derive a limit on the mass of the distant companion, yielding a value of M$_{\star}$ < 5,000 M$_{\odot}$ at a 95% confidence level.

This research delves into the solutions of SDEs where a fractional Brownian motion with a stabilizing function and Hurst parameter $H$ within the interval $(0,1)$ serves as the noise source. By establishing key outcomes, it begins with fundamental solution properties and continues with regularity and strong Markovian properties of solutions with respect to the initial data. Additionally, it proves that the solution has a continuous modification and explores relationships between $H$ and the large-scale behavior of SDE solutions, revealing distinct influences of H on these phenomena. Furthermore, it highlights how the characteristics of the stabilizing function impact the solution's characteristics, including its influence on the solution's H\"older index. Ultimately, it examines how the characteristics of the stabilizing function and $H$ interact to affect solution properties, including their influence on the presence of singularities, strong Markov property, and H\"older indices.

We have discovered that the nonstationary ideal on ω1 can be represented by
a Σ1 formula with a set parameter if and only if it is not preceded by
the quasideal Iλ for λ less than ω1. Consequently, the theory of
the nonstationary ideal is complete when expanded by its characteristic
formula, as this condition serves as a definitive and computable criterion
for the theory's completeness. Furthermore, the method employed in the proof
enables us to demonstrate that the theory of every quasideal Iλ, for λ less
than ω1, can be rephrased within ZFC's language and is consistent with it.

Multitask training can naturally leverage overcomplete representations by leveraging prior knowledge of related tasks, yet the benefits often remain unattainable due to the high costs of experimentation associated with training each task separately in sequence. To address this, we propose a novel Bayesian approach that allows for efficient multitask training by utilizing a hierarchical variational variational autoencoder with a latent task space. This approach is capable of jointly learning to infer task connections alongside the shared task structure within the latent space. We demonstrate that our method significantly reduces the computational expense of multitask training by at least 3 times the cost of sequential training, and it is particularly beneficial for tasks with high computational demands.

The development of large-scale datasets has significantly accelerated deep learning algorithms, enabling transfer learning to become more efficient. A notable example is the establishment of the German Traffic Sign dataset (GTSD), which has become the benchmark for evaluating traffic sign detection systems, especially those that utilize deep convolutional neural networks. This study examines the effectiveness of transfer learning by comparing the performance of systems trained using the GTSD with those trained using alternative datasets covering diverse environments. Furthermore, it investigates the impact of cross-country knowledge transfer and proposes a novel method to enhance the robustness of traffic sign detection systems, which can be applied to other object detection tasks.

Recommender systems have traditionally utilized collaborative filtering techniques to provide personalized suggestions based on user-item interactions. Although neural CF and graph neural CF have achieved impressive results, they often rely on costly and time-consuming supervised training processes. This paper introduces SelfCF, a novel framework that enables neural CF and GNNs to learn representation without relying on expensive supervised training data. By utilizing self-supervised contrastive learning, SelfCF effectively develops robust representations of users and items using the available interaction data. Moreover, SelfCF leverages a novel approach to integrate CF and GNNs by employing node embedding to preserve global item relationships in the item graph, resulting in superior recommendation performance. Experimental evaluations across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that SelfCF outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of recommendation accuracy and training efficiency.

The problem of counting covers of a curve by a genus g cover through smooth and ramified maps, with specified ramification conditions, dates back to the 19th century but remains largely unsolved, even in the case of genus g = 1, when it's a question of counting curves of a certain degree. However, in recent years researchers have made significant progress in this area, particularly through the use of Fabry-Buniakovsky's conjecture, which provides a formula for the number of covers of a curve by a genus g cover under specified conditions. This study builds on these earlier findings, extending Fabry-Buniakovsky's conjecture to cover covers of a genus g curve that intersect a divisor of a given degree and order. The research involves applying the intersection theory to understand how the geometry of the resulting covers influences the count, using a method called Gromov's problem as a reference, and it requires the use of a technique known as spectral pairs to resolve the problem. Furthermore, researchers have derived an equivalent version of this problem, in which the covers in question are not necessarily smooth but rather r-regular covers, and they have used this to establish a corresponding formula for the number of such covers that intersect a divisor of a given order and degree.

The high-energy properties of a gapped Dirac semimetal are investigated using an extended 8$\times$8 representation of the Dirac equation in a three-dimensional cubic lattice. The energy spectrum is divided into two parts: a gapless Dirac band and a gapped band, with the latter's properties being influenced by the 8-component spinor. The results show that the density of states and optical conductivity exhibit non-singular behavior at zero energy in a gapped Dirac semimetal. At high energies, a specific energy-independent energy law is obtained for the density of states and optical conductivity. In contrast, a singular energy law is observed in a massless Dirac gas. The study also reveals that the 8-component spinor of the gapped Dirac band contributes significantly to the density of states and optical conductivity at high energies.

We analyze the global behavior of a large class of population models with periodic coefficients, whose associated differential equations demonstrate both hyperbolic and singular perturbation characteristics. By establishing a complete semiflow in a specific space and a 2-positivity property for the corresponding problem, we derive several key conclusions, including the existence of global weak solutions, the well-posedness of the problem, and the upper semicontinuity of singular perturbation modes into the model's main equation.

Gravitational wave detectors are able to identify binary black hole mergers by analyzing unique patterns in their waveforms, but low signal strength in existing equipment makes it challenging to detect certain modes. This study explores the potential to identify binary black hole events in upgraded detectors, focusing on the third-generation Virgo detector and its capabilities. By simulating binary black hole mergers with varying masses and orientations, we discovered that upgraded detectors will be capable of detecting approximately 40% of binary events in the (3,3) and (4,4) modes. Furthermore, we found that events involving equal-mass black holes will be more prevalent in limited single-detector observations and multi-detector networks, but will be less prevalent in broader networks. This study's findings suggest that future gravitational wave observations may be able to identify binary black hole events in the near future, paving the way for further research into binary black hole characteristics.

A comprehensive investigation into astrometric binaries was conducted, examining a total of 1,111 systems, with a focus on identifying potential candidates featuring a black hole companion through a combination of statistical methods and kinematic analysis. These candidates were divided into three distinct groups: 68 systems with a brown dwarf or low-mass star in a close orbit, 63 systems with a brown dwarf companion, and 980 systems with a stellar companion. To enhance the accuracy of our analysis, we employed a new method to calculate the probability of a binary system being bound. Our research uncovered 34 kinematically matched binary systems, with 14 of these being newly identified as potential astrometric binaries through our study. Furthermore, we discuss the intriguing characteristics of these binary systems, with particular attention to three systems: a close binary with an exceptionally high orbital period of 20 years, a binary system with a low-mass primary and a late-type secondary, and a binary system with a brown dwarf companion that poses challenges for theoretical models of its formation.

To effectively apply the (1+1) evolutionary algorithm to a zero-one knapsack problem, we must strike a balance between crossover and selection through suitable parameter adjustments. We have conducted an extensive study, analyzing the effectiveness of six crossover methods combined with eight selection methods. By means of the fixed knapsack instance approach and the hyperball model, we have identified the optimal combinations of crossover and selection methods that produce the highest convergence rate, relying on the hyperball model's estimated lower bound on the convergence time. The findings indicate that the combination of uniform crossover and the F1 selection method achieves the highest convergence rate, while the 1/4 uniform crossover paired with the F2 selection method comes close.

This study examines the $L^2$ quantification of a specific type of integral, specifically oscillatory integrals with a parameter-dependent frequency vector, whose corresponding phase function is a linear combination of vectors.  The research yields two main outcomes: Firstly, it demonstrates that the $L^2$ quantification of these oscillatory integrals with linear phase functions is comparable to that of those with polynomial phase functions.  Secondly, it extends the previously established 2D and 3D decoupling inequalities of the decoupling inequality of Bourgain, Gan, and Li to a parameter-dependent setting. The research relies heavily on a refined version of the decoupling lemma of Bourgain, Gan, and Li.

The automatic identification of hate speech is a complex task that involves analyzing various forms of language for signs of aggression, toxicity, and stereotyping. While previous studies have explored the use of machine learning to detect hate speech automatically, this project takes a different approach by employing advanced natural language processing models to analyze conversations on social media platforms. By combining these models with sophisticated training methods and retraining techniques, the experiment achieved promising results on three separate tasks: identifying hate speech at the sentence level, the conversation level, and the document level. On a comprehensive evaluation task, the experiment secured top rankings for two models, while achieving outstanding performance on a specific subtask. A closer examination of the results highlights areas where further improvement is needed.

Quantum Monte Carlo simulations are known for their global accuracy in predicting molecular properties but are often limited by the high computational cost associated with increasing atomic mass and complexity. Our research demonstrates a new, more efficient approach to quantum Monte Carlo simulations tailored for molecules with larger atomic masses. By separating the valence electrons from the core in molecular systems, we developed a method to leverage the cost benefits of core-pseudopotential approximations while maintaining or even improving the accuracy of the simulations. Our findings show that the computational cost of the simulations scales with the square of the valence electron count, which in turn depends on the effective pseudopotential valence charge, allowing for significant time and memory savings. Our implementation of the new method in the QMCPack code was used to simulate various large molecules, achieving a substantial reduction in computational time and memory usage.

The platform Twitter has been a primary means for users to share and discuss political information, but it has also been criticized for allowing users to spread false information, particularly in more extreme political contexts. In 2020, the platform played a significant role in disseminating claims about voter fraud after the US presidential election, which led to it blocking users who made such claims from posting on the platform. In a study of this context, a dataset of around 700,000 tweets about the US election and voters was created and two different approaches were used to analyze this data. This analysis involved examining the claims made about voter fraud and identifying the linguistic patterns associated with such claims as well as those made by users who spread these claims. In a further step, the study examined the behavior of users who spread these claims by looking at their past activity on the platform and found that around 30% of them went on to post on alternative social media platforms after being blocked.

We have demonstrated in this paper that primary characteristics of the SRB measure, 
including its divergence from positive Lebesgue measure, reliance on the 
uniqueness of the SRB measure, points of at most 2 together having a 
particular dimension of zero, and the set of recurrence points having a 
particular dimension of one, can be achieved in a wide range of chaotic 
systems. We achieved this by developing a new technique to approximate 
SRB measures with finite-dimensional simplicial complexes, characterized 
by being shift-invariant, finitely generated, and with a particular 
dimension of one.

We've developed a novel approach to approximate inference in deep Bayesian neural networks, by leveraging variational autoencoders to create efficient and high-capacity encoder circuits. By representing the posterior parameter distribution as a variational autoencoder's latent space, we can utilize basic backpropagation to train the encoder. By combining this encoder with a Gaussian distribution over parameters, we can obtain a tractable posterior parameter distribution. This framework offers flexibility in choosing the complexity of the encoder based on the specific problem at hand, thus allowing for adaptable inference. Furthermore, our method can be extended to account for additional latent factors such as noise and outliers. By incorporating these factors, we can obtain a more accurate posterior parameter distribution. We've also developed a generalization error metric for a regression task, which can be used to optimize the hyperparameters of the encoder circuit. Our approach has been tested on multiple datasets and has shown comparable performance to other deep Bayesian neural networks.

This article showcases a simplified approach to instanton theory that breaks down the barrier for investigating a broader range of dynamic processes. The theory is applied to understand reaction mechanisms underlying electron transfer and superconductivity. Furthermore, it is demonstrated how instanton theory can be used to infer kinetic isotope effects based on quantum mechanical calculations. Lastly, the article highlights potential applications of instanton theory to further analyze reaction dynamics in chemistry and physics.

A straightforward method for achieving stable trajectory tracking is presented for systems of different types. Current methods for tracking control often rely on precise models, but in reality, various uncertainties and disturbances can lead to poor performance and instability. In contrast, this method uses feedback control without relying on process models, but instead requires a model of the desired overall system behavior, which can be easily obtained from tracking existing controllers. The proposed method ensures the overall system behavior stays consistent, regardless of tracking errors. The method is applied to a specific case of tracking unstable nonlinear systems and is verified through computer simulations.

This research investigates the effects of tungsten impurities on the electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties of an alloy consisting of vanadium and tungsten. The presence of a tungsten-based impurity band leads to a reduction in electrical conductivity and thermoelectric coefficients. The impurity band interacts with the magnetic subsystem, which is primarily influenced by the formation of V$_2$O$_5$ magnetic clusters. The interaction between the magnetic clusters and the tungsten impurity band is a key factor in understanding the behavior of the alloy. The alloy's electronic structure and magnetic properties are comparable to those of a specific compound (Ca-doped vanadium oxide), which is a prime material for the construction of high-temperature superconducting nanocostals.

The classic problem of perfect sums can be reduced to a non-linear binary integer programming issue. We suggest an efficient solution using a probabilistic method. The proposed algorithm iteratively selects binary variables according to their probability of contributing to a solution summing to the target value. We calculate these probabilities through linear combinations of binary variable products and analyze their convergence when the input is randomly generated. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional methods like branch-and-bound in both precision and speed. Furthermore, it proves more resilient to input perturbations compared to existing methods.
